entry.title: Zwift announces Zwift Plus premium subscription with real world video and adaptive coaching
entry.content:
Cyclist
Zwift announces Zwift Plus premium subscription with real world video and adaptive coaching

Zwift has launched a premium tier to its indoor training app. For a monthly fee that increases to £26.99 / $29.99 / €29.99 from the standard Zwift’s £17.99 / $19.99 / €19.99 per month subscription price, with Zwift Plus offering riders high definition real world cycling routes and personalised training plans.

Real world video on Zwift

For the first time, Zwift will offer real world video routes to Zwift Plus users. 

It says that initially there will be 21 routes with 385km of roads including the Col du Galibier, Sa Calobra, Cime de la Bonnette, Teide plus routes in Norway, South Africa, Utah, Colorado and the Scottish Highlands.

Zwift incorporates its standard add-ons, including PowerUps, segment leaderboards and race-oriented arches and road graffiti, while its ride physics is ported over onto the new roads. It promises new real road video in 2027.

The switch from virtual to real worlds in Zwift is one of the first fruits of Zwift’s purchase of Rouvy in April this year, as it looks to be progressively integrating the two platforms more closely. Although they currently still require separate subscriptions, rides on Rouvy can count towards Zwift credits and vice versa.

Zwift Plus adaptive training plans

Standard training plans are prescriptive and can be difficult to stick to if you have other commitments. They also risk boredom and burnout. 

Zwift says that its new Zwift Coach plans, also included as part of the Zwift Plus subscription, adapt to your schedule and use Zwift’s full training content library to offer a plan personalised to your goals and based on your recent fitness and your ride preferences. There’s a simple Q&A in the Zwift app to get you started and define your plan, and the app will then recommend which workout to complete next and explain why it’s been selected.

Zwift’s analysis shows that 63% of its users take part in a range of activities, with only 13% purely using the platform to complete structured workouts. 

Zwift says its plans are based on a sports science-based training model, while leveraging anonymised Zwift data on power and heart rate from Zwift’s millions of users to propose your next workout and how hard it should be. 

It claims that the Zwift Coach functionality will combine structured workouts with rides and events in the app, with RoboPacers to help keep you on track. It’s designed to allow you to skip a day if you need to recover or if you’ve decided to take it outdoors.

Post workout, there’s immediate feedback in Zwift via a new Coach Analysis tab in the activity report screen, with the analysis subsequently available in the Zwift companion app. 

Adaptive training isn’t unique to Zwift Coach, with TrainerRoad a competitor that offers an adaptive schedule that assesses performance after each workout and adapts your future schedule accordingly, also compensating for missed workouts.  

Indoor cycling shake-up

Indoor cycling looks to be having a shake-out this year. Not only has Zwift bought Rouvy, but Garmin bought TrainingPeaks in July, while some niche apps such as BKool – which was acquired by Rouvy last year – have disappeared.   

TrainingPeaks offers premium tiers with differing frequency of interactions with a real-world coach. Wahoo too offers multiple tiers, from free-of-charge ride recording from its Elemnt bike computers through to personalised workouts and access to its Sufferfest videos.

MyWhoosh too has been enhancing its offering, which for now remains free to use. It claims to have the second largest user base after Zwift and is adding 59km of new island-based roads, as well as an enhanced workout selector and a new way to earn rewards by riding. There are also new Zombie Workouts, where you’re incentivised to hit your target power by chasing zombies. There’s also an opportunity to ride with Tadej Pogačar this Saturday. 

Zwift has also been inspired by islands, just this week adding 17km to its virtual worlds based on Catalina Island in Southern California. Last month, it launched version 2 of its Zwift Ride indoor bike frame, while Rouvy is now compatible with Zwift Cog and Click and is adding video from far-flung locations to its library.

For a limited period, Zwift Plus is available free for one month to existing Zwift subscribers and there’s a 14-day trial for new subscribers.

The post Zwift announces Zwift Plus premium subscription with real world video and adaptive coaching appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: New Zwift+ Tier Goes Premium w/ Real-World Videos & Zwift Coach to Offer Personalized Training Guidance
entry.content:
Once again, I found myself in the peculiar situation of being invited to a real-world bucket-list riding destination by a virtual cycling platform. This time, Zwift was hosting us out in Moab, UT. I didn’t know what to expect, other than we were told to bring road cycling gear.

So I headed off to the desert, only to be met with a deluge of rain. The same storm system that forced the cancellation of the men’s Red Bull Rampage and the Moab 240 Trail Race was still dumping rain in and around Moab. No matter, this was for Zwift, right? The indoor virtual cycling program?

Yes. But there was a reason we were in Moab – to ride a new route, both virtually and in real life.

Zwift Video

You see, Zwift has an all-new premium tier they’re calling Zwift+. And one of the two main features of Zwift+ is Zwift Video. These are real-life videos of legendary rides turned into virtual riding courses. If you’re thinking this sounds an awful lot like Rouvy, you’d be right. That’s also one of the reasons Zwift recently bought Rouvy.

Don’t worry Rouvy fans. Zwift promises that the Rouvy platform isn’t going anywhere. They also claim that they had started the Zwift Video project as a hackathon project internally before even considering the acquisition. But through the development process, it just seemed to make sense, so now Rouvy is owned by Zwift but operates independently.

What’s interesting here is that according to Zwift, there is currently just a 2% overlap between Rouvy users and Zwift users. Because of that, they still don’t see a lot of crossover between the two platforms, and Zwift wanted to make their video platform unique.

It still uses high-quality video of extraordinary rides to offer an immersive riding experience, but they added all of the Zwift features you expect out of the animated world for a workout that rides and plays like Zwift, but looks like Rouvy.

Zwifters are always asking for more tarmac (and gravel), so at launch, Zwift Video will deliver 21 new routes from six destinations. In total, there are 385km of new pavement, broken pavement, and gravel, in all season from sunrise to sunset. The routes range from short 6.2km bursts to 29km rides with 38-1055m elevation gains.

The complete list of Zwift Video destinations and routes available at launch:

  • The French Alps: Col du Galibier (Lautaret), Cime de la Bonette, Upper Bonette 
  • Mallorca: Sa Calobra, Coll de Femenia 
  • Tenerife: Teide Plateau 
  • Western Cape: Chapmans Peak, Clarence Drive, Bain’s Kloof Pass, Du Toitskloof Pass 
  • Lofoten Islands: The Midnight Sun Road, Eggum Coastal, Nappvang Glow 
  • Southern Utah: The Hogsback, Arches National Park, Glen Canyon, Colorado River Sunrise
  • Colorado: Dolores Dirt 
  • The Scottish Highlands: Glen Etive, Quinag Highlands, Glen Garry Wilds

Each video was filmed specifically for Zwift, and filmed in high definition, with a high frame rate, and vehicle speed to make it all look flawless at cycling speeds. When the Zwift team came to Utah in March, they drove thousands of kilometers to find the best roads, and settled on four routes. Lest you think it was as simple as just driving along and filming each route, one of Zwift’s employees even had to write an app to tell the driver how fast to drive in order to film at the best frame rate for cycling. They also had to contend with other vehicles and people on the routes, all while trying to film with the best lighting conditions. The results speak for themselves, but it’s clear that Zwift put a lot of effort into this.

The purpose of this trip was to ride the Colorado River Sunrise route in Zwift, and then ride it in real life the next day. Unfortunately, the weather had other plans for us, so I’ll just have to go back to Moab sometime to check it off the list. Darn.

I can also ride that route at home, albeit a shorter 15.2-mile version of it one way. Once you get to the end of that route (or any Zwift Video route), you hit a transfer portal that takes you back to the start so you can lap it as many times as you want. Just like regular Zwift worlds, you can do any prescribed workouts in the Zwift Video routes. You’ll also be sharing the routes with anyone who happens to be on that route at the same time, just like the rest of Zwift. Organized rides and MeetUps won’t be available at launch, but will be introduced in the coming months.

New Roads and destinations will be added regularly, and if you’re up for the Globetrotter Challenge, riding 10 different routes between now and February will gain you the Globetrotter kit and bonus XP.

Want to ride Zwift Video routes? They will only be available to those who pay for the new premium Zwift+ tier.

Zwift Coach

The other thing you’ll get in that premium Zwift+ tier is access to the new Zwift Coach.

At this point, Zwift has mountains of indoor training data with 88 million indoor activities in just the past year. Zwift is apparently often people’s first interaction with cycling, and their fastest-growing category is beginner and recreational cyclists. Along those lines, cycling coaching can be intimidating – many riders think they’re not serious enough, can’t afford it, etc.

Zwift doesn’t see Zwift Coach replacing traditional cycling coaches, but sees it as another tool that cyclists can use along their journey with approachable training advice. After all, the most effective workout is the one you actually do – again, Zwift has the data to back it up. Riders on a Zwift plan gained roughly twice the FTP of riders with no plan, and those who ride at least twice per week are 2.8x fitter than those who ride once every two weeks. And Zwifters with a 12-week streak see 6-12% gains in FTP.

Clearly, structure pays off, but a lot of riders don’t know what that structure should be. That’s where Coach comes in. Stating that training should adapt to your life, not the other way around, you simply set a goal, and Coach does the rest. With all the hype around AI, you may be expecting this to just be Zwift-ified ChatGPT, but Zwift states that the program uses a science-based training model using their collection of indoor ride data (claimed to be the largest in the world) to build a mathematical training guide.

That’s not to say that Zwift Coach doesn’t use AI. Instead of using AI to build the plan, they use AI to take the mathematically built plan and then explain it to you and present it in a way that’s easy to understand.

To start using Coach, you’ll create a training plan on the Zwift Companion App and answer a number of questions to determine what you want to focus on, how long you want the plan to be (2 weeks – 6 months max), what days you can work out, and other details to personalize the training program. Once you create the plan, Zwift Coach will sit right on the home screen to give you daily guidance with today’s activities and your week ahead.

As soon as you finish a ride, you’ll be given post-ride feedback on how you performed, the duration, focus, and cumulative stress score, what comes next, and you’ll gain XP and Drops for the effort to help keep you motivated.

If you miss a day, decide it’s too hard, etc., the training program will adapt – though currently you have to physically press a button to tell it to Adapt Plan.

The plan will (soon) also take into account rides done outside and runs, though Zwift was quick to point out that this is not a running coach. We’ve been given early access to Zwift+ and Zwift Coach, but since we’re using it in a walled-off version of the Companion app in TestFlight and a downloaded offline version of Zwift, it didn’t get leaked early; it’s hard to say what functionality is lacking because of that or what’s just not ready yet. I have the option of adding outdoor workouts, but once added, it doesn’t seem to show up anywhere unless you schedule it for the future. Eventually, you should be able to add outdoor workouts that you completed in the past and have that impact your training program.

Along those lines, expect Coach to improve along with your cycling performance. Zwift is already planning to add alternative workouts, more personalization, and a Coach Chat feature that will allow you to ask what you need to do and why to do it.

Zwift gave two examples of external testers who used Zwift Coach, and their results were pretty impressive. One century rider was training for a specific event and used it for a 4.5-week Coach plan that saw their fitness (CTL) increase by 18%, while their FTP went up from 246W to 259W on event day, and continued up to 275W for the full plan. Another rider hoped to level up to group B with an FTP increase, and used a 15-week Coach plan to see their FTP increase from 178W to 210W, an increase of 18%.

Obviously, you have to put in the work. But Zwift Coach seems like a great way to turn your goal into actionable workouts. It’s important to note that Zwift has pledged to remain a fully open platform, even with Zwift Coach – all existing and new coaching products that integrate with Zwift will continue to do so.

Zwift+ / Zwift Pricing, and How to Access Video & Coach

There’s a lot that went into the development of Zwift Video and Zwift Coach. In fact, they had to create an entirely new team at Zwift to devote to Zwift+, now with 300 people working on various aspects of the program. So, to make it all work financially, you’ve gotta pay. Currently, Zwift Video and Zwift Coach are only available in the new Zwift+ premium tier. Zwift+ is $29.99 per month, and includes everything you get out of normal Zwift plus the Video and Coach features.

For those who aren’t interested in Video or Coach and still want to use Zwift, the standard Zwift tier will still be available for $19.99 per month. At launch, existing Zwift users can opt into a limited-time one-month free trial of Zwift+, while completely new users can get a 14-day free trial before having to purchase.

There are no plans for any dual Zwift/Rouvy memberships, mostly because it doesn’t sound like Zwift expects there to be demand. So if that’s something you’d be into, speak up.

Regular Zwift Updates

But wait, there’s more! In addition to Zwift+, the standard Zwift world is receiving a number of updates, including a refreshed home screen with a cleaner, simpler layout, a new progress widget, a Zwift Companion home screen update, Oura ring integration, deeper Whoop integration, and a Watt Lock feature to allow you to stick to a specific wattage during freeride mode.

For the route hunters, Zwift is adding another Watopia expansion with a three-island archipelago inspired by California’s coast and Catalina Island. The update adds about 17km of flat, fast roads with ocean views and new wildlife. Two of the islands are built with crit racing in mind, and the new roads provide a bypass around the Mayan Jungle to create a longer, flatter route. At launch, there will be 9 new cycling routes and 3 running routes, including Caldera Coaster, Seafoam Circuit, and Pacific Pursuit, all live from day one along with Stage 4 of The Tour of Watopia.

zwift.com

entry.title: Yakima’s OnRamp LX Hitch Rack Isn’t the Simplest, but It’s Sturdy, Adaptable, and Hauls eBikes
entry.content:
After acquiring a vehicle that won’t fit a bike inside, I’ve become reliant on hitch racks to move my bikes around. This Spring, I got the offer to test the OnRamp LX 2-bike hitch rack from Yakima. This rack offers a 70 lbs. per bike capacity and a detachable ramp to roll heavier bikes (like ebikes) onto its trays. The rack uses stabilizers to hold your bikes’ frame or seatpost, so it can carry bikes with fenders.

While the OnRamp LX is slightly less user-friendly than other racks, its weight capacity, adaptability to different bikes, and stability on my vehicle all impressed me. Any of the rack’s inconveniences are pretty minor, and in my eyes forgivable in exchange for its trustworthy construction and reliable operation.  

Yakima OnRamp LX – Key Specs:

The OnRamp LX carries two bikes, with a max. capacity of 70 lbs. per tray (or 80 lbs. for the 2” receiver model), so it’s a great option for moving ebikes or eMTBs. I tested the 1 ¼” model, and the rack itself weighs 53.5 lbs.

The rack’s trays accommodate tires up to 5” wide, wheels up to 32” diameter, and wheelbases up to 54”. The OnRamp LX’s stabilizers clamp to your bikes’ frame or seatpost, so fenders are no problem and the rack should accommodate nearly any bike.

Yakima’s hitch pin comes with a lock so the rack can’t be removed from your vehicle. The OnRamp LX does not include a lock for your bikes, but any cable lock can be looped around the rack’s frame and your bikes. When not in use, the rack folds up vertically and takes up little space.

Assembly/Adjustments:

Assembling the OnRamp LX was an easy job. Once you’ve installed a single bolt that joins the tongue portion to the rest of the rack, the rack is fully assembled! Attaching the rack to your vehicle only requires you to slip the tongue into the receiver, screw in the hitch pin, and put the lock on the end of the pin.

The only thing I’ll note is the hitch pin must be installed tightly (100 Nm). Yakima supplies wrenches, but they’re thin and not easy on the hands. I used a socket wrench on the hitch pin, partly to ensure it was tight enough, but also because my vehicle and hitch don’t leave a lot of room around the pin. I used Yakima’s wrench to install the bolt that joins the rack to its tongue, but that bolt took a fair bit of torque, so a socket wrench would make that job easier too.

Now the rack is complete and attached to your vehicle, but there are a few adjustments you’ll have to make to ensure your bikes fit on it properly. First, you’ll want to adjust the length of the trays so your wheels fit securely against the chocks. You also need to make sure your bikes are centered on your vehicle.

Adjusting one end of the tray is easy and tool-free, but for the first bikes I loaded (my MTB and a commuter bike), I did have to move the bolted-in half of both trays to get the bikes centered. This requires the removal of one Allen bolt per tray, and only takes a few minutes.

From step one of assembly to having two bikes loaded with all the necessary adjustments made, it took me one hour and 15 minutes – and I was in no rush.

Once your trays are adjusted, you’re ready to load bikes. The namesake feature of the OnRamp LX is a detachable ramp that allows you to simply roll heavier bikes up and onto the tray. When not in use, the ramp attaches to the rack so it’s always there if needed. The only catch with the ramp is that you need to have the space to use it. I have a single-car driveway, so I’d have to pull my car out to attach and utilize the ramp. In parking lots, the vehicle next to you could be in the way.

Loading Bikes/Ease of Use:

Securing bikes is fairly easy, but there’s one awkward moment when you’re loading a bike onto the inner tray: You have to hold your bike upright with one hand while you raise the rack’s mast, get one of the stabilizers positioned to hold your frame or seatpost, and buckle its strap around your bike. This isn’t terribly tricky to do, but racks that hold the bike’s wheel(s) are easier to load. Loading bikes on the OnRamp LX’s outside tray is slightly easier since the mast will be raised already.

It’s up to you to decide where you want to put the stabilizer, but I had no trouble finding good places on the frames or seatposts to hold all the bikes I hauled. I’d recommend getting as close to the top tube/seat mast junction as possible, but I clamped my lighter commuter bike on the down tube for a short drive, and it was perfectly stable.

One thing I’ll mention is to be sure to tighten the stabilizers snugly on the mast; On my first load, I thought I had one tight, but it suddenly moved. It took a few more turns of the knob to get the stabilizer properly secured.

After this, it’s just a matter of strapping both your bike’s wheels down to the trays. The straps must be positioned at outward 45° angles, but the buckles are fixed in that position so you can’t go wrong. Finally, Yakima does supply a strap to put around your bikes for extra security (and they recommend using it every time). They simply instruct you to strap it around both frames and the rack’s mast. The strap is basically a fail-safe in case something breaks or a bike is loaded incorrectly – It could prevent bikes from falling right off the rack.

Removing bikes is mostly an easy job, but there’s another tricky moment when you’re taking the bike off the inner tray. When that bike comes off, you’ll want to drop the mast out of the way. This involves holding the bike up while unbuckling and loosening the stabilizer, then pulling a pin at the bottom of the mast and pushing the mast sideways. Thankfully, just a nudge on the mast is enough to disengage the clip that holds it upright.

When the mast goes down, you’ll also have to re-position the stabilizers so they don’t interfere with the trays. This means you can’t position a stabilizer to hold your bike and leave it there – It has to be repositioned every time the mast goes up and down.

Aside from loading and unloading bikes, the OnRamp LX isn’t the quickest or easiest rack to use in a few other ways. First off, it does require tools to remove it from your vehicle. If you regularly take your rack on and off, a tool-free mechanism like Thule’s Verse rack offers is a nicer option… however, some people might prefer the security of Yakima’s screw-in hitch pin. The Thule Verse also has the OnRamp LX beat in terms of adjusting to different wheelbases. Its simple sliding wheel chocks are quicker and easier than adjusting tray lengths.

Bike Compatibility:

Throughout the summer, I carried at least five different bikes on the OnRamp LX, including a commuter bike, an e-commuter, multiple MTBs, and two eMTBs. The rack’s ‘Stadium Seating’ trays sit at staggered heights, so I had no problems loading any of these bikes securely, and only one minor interference between two of them. With my commuter bike and MTB on the rack, I had to move the seat on my commuter so it didn’t touch my MTB’s handlebars. Aside from that, all the bikes I hauled were safely separated on the OnRamp LX.

When I loaded up my Priority ebike, I did have to shorten the tray length for its wheelbase. Thankfully, the end of the tray you can adjust by hand-spinning a knob afforded enough adjustment, so it was a quick job with no tools required. Being able to carry bikes with fenders was great – Those stabilizers are a bit finicky to operate versus wheel holders, but their compatibility with bikes is excellent.

Driving:

Something I liked right away about the OnRamp LX is how little it sticks out when it’s folded up. The folded rack only protrudes about 8” from my car’s bumper, which is great when you’re parking in tighter spots. With my car, I can’t even see the top of the rack over my trunk, so it doesn’t impede visibility at all when folded up. The trunk of my car will easily open with the rack upright, and in most cases I could still open it with bikes on the rack. Folding the rack up and down is easy: There’s a spring-loaded pin on one side and a backup pin that pops in and out on the other.

The only potential issue with leaving the rack up depends on your vehicle…, but in my case the tray blocks my license plate! Thankfully, even when left down, the rack doesn’t stick out too far, so it’s totally reasonable to drive with it down and keep your plate visible. I was able to leave my car in several parking spots with the rack down, without going outside the lines.

As for rear visibility with bikes on the rack, the OnRamp LX holds bikes high enough that they do take up most of my rearward view. However, it’s not difficult to see what’s happening behind you even when you’re looking through two bikes.

I found another potential concern, but everything was OK in my case: The front wheel of the bike on the OnRamp LX’s inside tray sits close to my exhaust pipes. After one early drive, the rack felt a bit warm, so I kept an eye on this. Fortunately, after several longer drives, I never had a tire get warm, let alone hot.

Stability/Reliability:

I found the OnRamp LX to be a stable and very trustworthy rack. Immediately, I liked the square-framed design, which looks very sturdy. The threaded hitch pin holds the rack tightly to the receiver, and even if it loosens up, the pin lock should keep it from falling out.

Your bikes will do some side-to-side wiggling when driving bumpy roads, but the OnRamp LX resisted movement slightly better than the Thule rack I tested last year. I had no concerning wobbles travelling a few miles on a washboarded gravel road with my 53 lbs. ebike on the rack, or anytime I had two bikes loaded up.

I did notice the front wheel of my MTB was wiggling back and forth slightly while I drove – The wheel straps are not very flexible, and they don’t sit perfectly flat against my rim. The straps never loosened up, but they do allow some wheel wiggle in high winds.

After a whole summer on my car with regular use, I have no concerns about durability or reliability with the OnRamp LX. I’ve had no functional issues with the rack; there’s no excessive wear and tear to report, nothing has loosened up, and I trust it to carry my bikes safely.

The Yakima OnRamp LX hitch rack retails for $999.00.

yakima.com

entry.title: Chromag’s Limber MTB Saddle Provides Plenty of Support in a Trim Package
entry.content:
Chromag Bikes started building their brand on hardtail frames, but as components came along, they quickly became Whistler, B.C.’s unofficial handlebar of choice, then put out some very popular seats. Back in mid-June, Chromag Bikes announced their new Limber seat. This saddle was designed to be easy to move around when you’re standing up, but comfortable enough when you’re seated for long rides.

A few years ago I would have called Chromag’s Lynx DT saddle my current favourite, so I was stoked to try out the new Limber. I’ve been riding the Limber since its release, and despite facing a tough comparison to my favourite seat ever (Ergon’s SMC Core), I found it perfectly comfortable. The Limber is a nicely supportive saddle that maintains a sleek overall profile and a reasonable weight.

Chromag Limber Saddle – Construction Features:

Chromag says the new Limber was based upon their Lift saddle, but refined with a shorter profile and a broader center relief channel. The Limber’s vacuum-formed construction enables a seamless finish and a consistent surface feel. It features a durable, weather-resistant synthetic cover, and its design leaves no exposed plastic or sharp edges. Chromag gave the Limber chromoly rails for strength and durability without excess weight.

The Limber saddle offers a short 260mm length and movement-friendly shape to allow riders to shift around it easily, while a stable but not bulky 140mm platform width provides comfort when you are seated.

This saddle’s padding is on the thinner, firmer side, but the Limber’s design is all about proper support. Its platform was shaped to support the sit bones, where the bulk of your body weight hits the saddle. It also gets a widened center relief channel to keep pressure off sensitive areas and eliminate unnecessary discomfort. 

The Limber’s cover features a semi-perforated texture on the rear part of the platform and on the nose for a little grip, and remains smooth everywhere else.

When I installed the Limber saddle on my bike, I noticed the rails offer about 5mm less forward/back adjustability vs. the Ergon SMC Core seat I was previously riding (which is a larger seat). To match the Ergon’s position, I had to run the Limber as far forward as its clamp range allows, but that put it exactly where I wanted.

Chromag lists the Limber saddle’s weight at 278g. I’d call that honest, as my scale showed it at 279g. That’s 14g lighter than my old Lynx DT, and shaves 65g off the Ergon SMC Core’s weight.

Ride Impressions: Comfort

My first ride with the Limber saddle was a 1:45 long lap, and I was wearing my well-padded 7mesh MK3 chamois. Even after switching from a very cushy saddle, the Limber was more comfortable than expected. I attribute this to its shape more than anything; The rear half of this seat is wide enough to support my sit bones really well. I should note, I’m a fairly slim guy, but the Limber’s width was easily adequate for me.

My next ride was with a slimmer chamois, and since I was still getting used to it, the Limber felt a bit firm initially. However, I quickly stopped thinking about it as I rode, and I remained comfortable throughout this hour and a half long ride.

Just my third ride with the Limber was over three hours long. After two hours of climbing, my descent, and a lengthy pedal home, my butt was just starting to get a bit tired of sitting. Given I was still getting used to the Limber, I was pretty happy to complete this longer lap with no discomfort or soreness afterwards.

At this point I have ridden countless loops with the Limber saddle, and I’ve gotten familiar with it. Honestly, the Limber’s lean padding simply won’t match up to my Ergon SMC Core, which is amazingly cushy and comfortable. But since the sit bone support is excellent with the Limber, I still find it very comfortable and have no complaints about it. Through all my test rides, I’ve never had any specific comfort-related issues with this seat. Also, I have luckily never had problems with this, but the Limber’s wide center channel definitely kept my sensitive bits happy with no numbness at all.

Shape:

As stated above, my favourite thing about the Limber’s shape is its supportive rear half. That said, the nose worked really well for me too. I don’t like saddles with wide noses, and the Limber’s is narrow enough that I found it perfectly comfortable to pedal with. If a seat’s nose is too wide, I will feel like it’s pushing my thighs apart, but this was not a problem with the Limber.

While the Limber’s nose is noticeably shorter than the seat I was riding, that doesn’t seem to come with any sacrifice in comfort. The shorter nose also proved pretty good at not snagging the crotch of any of my various shorts or MTB pants. I’ll attribute this to the shape, but also the synthetic cover material. It’s grippy enough to not feel slippery, so when you plant your butt on the seat it doesn’t shift around. Thankfully, the cover isn’t grabby enough that it hooks up on clothing.  

Chromag wanted this seat to be easy to move around while you ride, and I’d agree it is. It’s just big enough to be supportive, and I never found it obtrusive or noticed my legs contacting it unexpectedly. The seat’s trim dimensions help it stay out of the way during stand-up pedalling sprints and on descents.

Durability:

Sorry, but I haven’t crashed hard or bounced my bike off a trail since installing the Limber saddle! After a few months of riding my seat shows no signs of damage, or excessive wear and tear. The rails are straight, the cover is fully intact, and I doubt anything would damage this seat except for a gnarly crash.

The Limber saddle retails for $110 USD. It is available in Black/Sand (as tested) or Chocolate colors. Chromag covers all their components with a two-year warranty.

chromagbikes.com

entry.title: Ornot Alpha Wool Pullover
entry.content:
Ornot uses Polartec Alpha in a few of their pieces, and we’ve become big fans of the material. Now, Polartec has a new Alpha Wool Fabric that combines wool’s natural properties with the high-tech performance of the original synthetic Alpha. You can have your cake and eat it too. Ornot is one of the few companies that has been granted early access to the material, so this is quite exciting news if fabrics and textures are your jam. Read below for all the details.

Ornot Wool Pullover Quick Hits:

  • 54% Poly, 6% Nylon, 40% Wool
  • Available in Men’s and Women’s silhouettes
  • Excellent warmth-to-weight ratio
  • Abrasion-resistant fabric in high-wear areas
  • Resists moisture and dries fast
  • Loose, casual fit
  • Sewn by hand in the USA
  • Colors: Fog/Ochre
  • MSRP: $198

Alpha Wool

Alpha with Wool is a brand new development from Polartec®. Made in the USA, this pullover takes the proven performance of Polartec® Alpha™ in a new direction, blending merino wool fibers into the lofted construction. Wool adds natural temperature regulation and moisture management, and makes this pullover so soft you’ll never want to take it off (ask us how we know). Purpose-built for stop-and-go efforts, like bike riding, where you need to dump heat quickly, the Alpha Wool Pullover merges the thermoregulation properties of Wool with the lightweight performance of Alpha™ Direct.

Originally adopted by thru-hikers, Alpha™ Direct is so lightweight it feels almost magical. This next-gen version, made with Polartec Alpha™ with Wool, advances its properties for wear on your bike, Ornot.

See the Alpha Wool Pullover at Ornot, available in Men’s and Women’s cuts.

The post Ornot Alpha Wool Pullover appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Tailfin Cooks Up “Slow Riding” Waxed Canvas Bikepacking Setup in its R&D Kitchen
entry.content:
Look, if you’re rocking a Tailfin bikepacking system on your steed, there’s a good chance you bikepack “fast” or “ultra”. Like, you need your bikepacking gear minimal and strapped high and tight on your bike. Well, recently, Tailfin teased us with some work they’ve been doing in their R&D Kitchen that’s for the bikepackers out there who aren’t in a hurry to get to where they’re going.

Now, this is a one-off, prototype bag setup. And as of right now, it will not be going into production. So try not to get too excited.

Slowing Things Down…

Tailfin is best known for making bikepacking gear lighter, faster, and generally more aero than your average sleeping bag. So it’s kinda cool that its latest project is about slowing down, bringing a fishing rod, and not being in any hurry.

The project came out of Tailfin’s “R&D Kitchen,” a couple-times-a-year side gig for Tailfin’s prototyping department. The workshop sits next to the kitchen at HQ, so therefore “R&D Kitchen”.

The department’s day job is building prototypes for the R&D Division, which is the brand’s group of ultra athletes. The Kitchen projects have no commercial target. They’re about experimenting and having fun.

For this one, the team skipped the usual “lighter and faster” goal. Instead, they asked what they’d actually want to take on a trip built around the stops rather than the distance. Their answer was extra time and extra luxuries.

For the Love of Waxed Canvas…

The bags are the star here, as they should be. Product team member Theo designed a front bag designed around holding a film camera, complete with a pocket for a real paper map “for the romance of it.” So far, I love this…

Molly turned one pannier into an insulated cool bag for cold beers and a refrigerated picnic. What? She also made a separate bag for a small espresso maker. This is turning out to be spectacular…

Soft Goods Prototyper Callum redesigned the frame bag with flip-top closures instead of zips. And it’s split vertically rather than horizontally, with access at the front so you can dig around in it while riding.

1960s Japanese Touring!

The inspiration came from Callum’s research into 1960s Japanese touring photos, which led back to the French constructeurs, who built bikes, racks, and bags as one integrated system. Japanese builders refined the idea over the following decades. “The bags aren’t an afterthought,” Callum said. The result is a British take on that tradition.

But what about the bike? The bags are built around the new Singular Peregrine Mk5, a lugged steel bike from Sam Alison’s Singular Cycles. Alison launched the Peregrine in 2008, and it was arguably a gravel bike before the category had a name.

Tailfin made its own versions of two touring classics for it: low front panniers and a randonneur handlebar bag. Both use British waxed canvas that weathers naturally, plus the same mounting hardware and stability engineering as Tailfin’s race gear. Bristol tailor David Darby Minns, a friend of the team, supplied fabric samples and vintage tailoring inspiration.

This bike and bag system hits me right in the feels so hard. The color, the aesthetics, the fenders… I am a sucker for a good-lookin’ randoneurring rig. But sadly, it’s not a product that’s in development. Boo!!!

However, the light at the end of the tunnel is that Tailfin expects ideas from the project to inform future work. So, hopefully we will see some more waxed canvas.

Where to See It?

  • Kendal Mountain Festival, 19–22 November 2026, Kendal, UK.
  • Velofollies, 22–24 January 2027, Kortrijk Xpo, Belgium

Hit the link below for Tailfin products that are in production and ready to go.

TailFin.cc

entry.title: What if every rider had a digital clone? The next frontier of scouting, training, racing and recovery using data
entry.content:
Cyclist
What if every rider had a digital clone? The next frontier of scouting, training, racing and recovery using data

‘In an ideal world you’d have embedded sensors tracking processes in your blood. To really understand a cyclist,  a human, to see how they are responding to training, feeding and recovery, you need continuous markers. We’re not there yet, but the technology is emerging.’

That’s Scott Drawer, performance director of Netcompany Ineos. He’s talking about digital twins, which could be the future of cycling. As you’ll discover in this article, the advent of artificial intelligence and omics could transform what it means to be a world-class rider…

What is a digital twin?

IBM describes a ‘digital twin’ as a ‘dynamic, virtual replica of a physical object, system or process that stays connected to its real-world counterpart through two-way data flows’. The idea is that you use real-world data to simulate, monitor and predict how the real-world counterpart behaves via a virtual twin clone.

For instance, in healthcare, there’s ‘surgical rehearsal’ where a surgeon can virtually ‘cut’ a piece of heart tissue or place a catheter to treat an irregular heartbeat. The digital twin instantly simulates how the heart’s electrical paths will reroute, showing whether the procedure will cure the arrhythmia or cause a new problem.

Then there’s ‘drug response testing’. If a patient needs a medication that carries a minor risk of a cardiac side-effect, the clinician can apply the drug’s chemical profile to the patient’s digital twin. The twin simulates how the patient’s specific ion channels will react, flagging whether the drug is safe or likely to trigger a heart attack.

Healthcare is driving this to keep people out of hospital, but what has this to do with cycling? Well, sceptics might suggest that history shows therapeutic advancements (eg, the blood booster erythropoietin to treat anaemia) are inevitably rebooted as performance-boosters. But no, this is a legitimate transfer of technology that could cover all areas of performance cycling.

Identifying the next Froome

I dropped Drawer a line off the back of a press release from Swansea University earlier this year that announced a collaboration with the Ineos team ‘towards the development of digital twins for efficient talent identification in professional cycling’.

‘It’s a small project involving one PhD student who’s great with data and loves cycling,’ Drawer says. ‘There’s so much information available publicly these days. People post rides on Strava and results are easier to find. Even at a basic level useful signals are available online. The Swansea project is about developing tools that can gather and analyse that public information to help identify outliers and promising opportunities, although I’d call it a “lite digital twin”.’

Drawer says that young talent has become increasingly important in professional cycling and, though they were late to the development programme, a team won’t survive without that clear pathway from juniors to seniors.

‘There’s huge competition to identify riders with the greatest potential,’ he says. ‘Of course, scouts and agents have their place and will continue to do so – it’s through them that we discovered Benjamín Noval three years ago. But refining that process is key to progress.’

In 2025, the team signed Noval Junior at just 16 with the now 18-year-old set to race for the senior team in 2027. In September, Noval won both the junior road race and time-trial at the UCI World Championships in Montreal.

The signs are promising that Noval will have an impact at WorldTour level, although Drawer caveats that the relationship between junior joy and senior success is low. A digital twin might reduce the guesswork. As will the team’s headline sponsors.

The truth-seekers

‘By far the biggest impact for us in this space is our partnership with Netcompany,’ says Drawer. ‘The technological scale and capability that we can access is unique in this sport and other sports. Netcompany describes itself as the “orchestrator”, and I’d say that’s right.’

Core to the Danish’s company’s success is Pulse. This is its real-time, AI-driven platform that consolidates massive streams of data from ‘fragmented ecosystems’ into a single, operational interface.

Netcompany made its name in the aviation industry, where the Pulse platform is branded ‘Airhart’. It serves as the digital backbone for Heathrow, Munich and Copenhagen airports to orchestrate flights, baggage and passenger tracking.

‘Imagine a flight is delayed by a headwind,’ says Drawer. ‘The gate it was due to use is occupied, and a large group of passengers is building up in one part of the terminal. That chain of events affects ground staff, catering and passenger communications. Netcompany’s software helps coordinate all those moving parts so the airport can operate efficiently.’

Cycling is drowning in data. You have instrumented cranks, heart rate monitors, head units… But in the technological revolution, collecting data is the easy bit. It’s making sense of it for positive interventions that’s the tricky part. And that covers all areas of a professional team.

‘Look at how much software has evolved and is impacting cycling,’ says Drawer. ‘A sports director uses VeloViewer, while being fed video images of the race and a live feed from ProCyclingStats. It’s a blizzard of information, a blizzard of data, and you’re trying to make sense of it all for practical decisions. It’s the same with coaches, nutritionists, doctors, aerodynamicists… But just because you can measure something doesn’t mean it has value. You must organise your data and information for points of truth. That’s what Netcompany is brilliant at and I think we’ll start to see the benefits of our collaboration next season. Ultimately, before you even think about a digital twin, you must have quality data and deep insights.’

Painting a complete picture

That’s also where the likes of Irish outfit Orreco come in. Founded by Dr Brian Moore in 2010, the company uses their proprietary AI and years of sport-science knowledge to accelerate recovery, optimise performance and prolong an athlete’s career.

‘In the 90s, before launching Orreco, we started with a stopwatch, a lactate sensor, a Polar chest strap and a pencil,’ says Moore. ‘Now, we’re using Bayesian inference models, agentic AI, biomarkers and computer vision to track athlete readiness, recovery and injury prevention.’

Orreco worked with Drawer and the Netcompany Ineos team at altitude camps, and monitored rider response at Grand Tours. It has also collaborated with Newcastle United football team for years, plus the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks and the NFL’s Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

‘We also worked with Dr Pete Cunningham and the cyclors onboard Team Ineos Brittania in the America’s Cup,’ says Moore. ‘Those boys were pushing some monstrous numbers as they were providing all the power for the manoeuvres and rigging. They were effectively cycling in a carbon-fibre furnace with tremendous thermal stress given the position in the boat. It was impressive.’

Orreco’s five modules provide a view of athlete health. ‘Biomarkers’ uses bloodwork to assess stress, inflammation, recovery and readiness, helping staff decide when training changes or assessment may be needed. ‘Medical Notes’ centralises medical and physiotherapy records, case notes and athlete status, supporting rehabilitation tracking and return-to-play decisions.

Then you have ‘Recovery Lab’, which combines GPS workload, wellness, sleep, wearable data, biomarkers and testing to personalise recovery. ‘Motion Signal’ uses computer vision to detect movement changes that may indicate overload and inform conditioning or rehabilitation. Finally, there’s ‘Analytics and Reporting’, which brings performance data into dashboards to monitor trends, compare athletes and guide coaching and medical decisions.

When it comes to the bloodwork, all of this starts with a sample via the vein or a finger-prick. ‘We can then, for instance, track each rider against their own baseline over time,’ says Moore. ‘If a rider’s oxidative stress is climbing while their antioxidant levels are dropping, they flag it to the coach. The insights from the biomarkers might mean swapping a planned interval session for an easy spin and focusing on sleep and nutrition for 48 hours.’

Moore says they worked with one cyclist whose power files looked strong, but their blood showed sharp cellular stress and rising inflammation. They advised the coach to drop a planned three-day hard block and focus on recovery. A few days later, other riders in the training group on that same hard block came down with upper respiratory tract infections, while this athlete stayed healthy and was back hitting peak numbers the following week.

As for digital twins, the thought excites Moore, who highlights that there’s already some advanced work on digital twins around aerodynamics and bike fit. ‘But our focus is about the biological digital twin, which is about modelling how the rider’s body will virtually respond to an intervention’, he says. ‘We already work with omics data, like metabolomics, and we’re using frontier models to help simulate state changes. That level of detail all makes the digital twin more realistic. The goal is simple: if a rider does ‘X’ on stage 14, what will their recovery state look like the next morning? That allows teams to plan tactics around real physiology rather than guessing.’

You might have heard of metabolomics. This branch of omics was thrust into the cycling media’s consciousness when then UAE Team Emirates’ head of performance Iñigo San Millán (now at Athletic Bilbao FC) revealed he’d measured hundreds of thousands of metabolites in Tadej Pogačar’s blood. The results led to San Millan concluding that elite riders like the Slovenian possess a metabolic signature, a unique phenotype, that means they can absorb huge volumes of training.

In the case of Pogačar, specific biomarkers revealed how he not only recovered rapidly between stages but also between surges, explaining his ability to go and go again when climbing. ‘With this metabolomic work, we can see how interventions and personalised intensities of exercise and durations can help a rider,’ San Millán said.

Metabolic interventions

Ruben Robberechts is a researcher in exercise physiology at Hasselt University in Limburg. He has led his own metabolomic research that revealed the metabolic response to ‘excessive endurance exercise’ by studying seven riders at the 2023 Tour de France. That excessiveness comprised 3,404km and 56,482m of climbing, resulting in a total work output of around 75,500kJ.

(Note: Robberechts doesn’t reveal which team he shadowed but one of the co-authors, Koen Pelgrim, is a trainer at Soudal Quick-Step, so we speculate that the septet profiled included two-time world champion Julian Alaphilippe, while the eighth starter, Fabio Jakobsen, withdrew on Stage 12 due to a lingering shoulder injury from Stage 4.)

‘One of the major findings of the study explicitly linked serum L-carnitine status and fatigue,’ Robberechts says. L-carnitine is a naturally occurring substance made mainly by your liver and kidneys. It helps the body transport fat into cells’ mitochondria, where it can be used to produce energy. ‘Given our observation, L-carnitine supplementation may be a potent strategy to attenuate fatigue during the Tour de France.’

Robberechts also revealed significant depletion of numerous amino acids, including cysteine. Cysteine helps to ‘buffer’ or neutralise excess reactive oxygen species, which you produce in spades when exercising hard. ‘It’s why recovery shakes could include elevated levels of cysteine for multi-stage races,’ he says.

Robberechts’ findings also bridged two spheres: the clinical and the sporting. During the pandemic, it became clear that when a person contracted Covid, levels of the peptide GDF-15 (Growth Differentiation Factor-15) spiked, making it one of the most reliable laboratory indicators for how severe the disease would become.

GDF-15 release is a stress reaction, which is why Robberechts monitored its levels during the 2023 study as well as an earlier one in 2019: ‘We noted its rise is a useful biomarker to gauge when overreaching might tip over into overtraining.’

Interestingly his earlier research also revealed that ketone supplementation blunted the GDF-15 response in the third week of the Tour. As high levels suppress appetite, the riders consumed more calories, which historically drop during the latter stages due to the intense training and fuelling regime. That doesn’t signal the green light for recreational riders to whip out their credit cards for a ketone bump, of course, as these GDF-15 levels only remain significantly high after days and days and etc, of hard riding.

It does, however, highlight that such detailed biological insight can actually lead to practical interventions: ‘And I feel this is just the start,’ Robberechts says. ‘We used the dried spot technique for blood collection, which is almost imperceptible, requires just a droplet or two of blood, and doesn’t require fridge storage.’ All reasons why it’s now used in anti-doping circles.

Rise of the biotech bikers

Made of Genes is another AI-powered biomedical intelligence company from Spain, who either take a swab or blood sample that contributes to a ‘digital twin that combines what never changes, such as genetics, with what shifts every day: internal biology, training and racing load, heart-rate variability, sleep, nutrition, travel and schedule,’ says the company’s founder Laura Isus. 

Made of Genes has worked with Spanish UCI ProTeam Equipo Kern Pharma and extensively with Barcelona’s women’s football team. Earlier this year, both outfits, plus the University of Bonn, announced they’d developed an AI framework to anticipate injuries in elite women’s football. Analysing four seasons of data from 34 players, it identifies cumulative fatigue and workload as key risk factors, helping medical and coaching staff personalise rest and improve player availability.

‘Our models are tested retrospectively and then prospectively by making predictions before they happen and checking them against real outcomes and against decisions the staff would have made without the model,’ Isus explains. ‘In elite football, our injury watchlist flagged more than 70% of non-contact injuries ahead of time, giving medical staff a window to act before injury happened.’

According to their statistics, they prevented 22.7% of injuries, meaning 20 days greater availability per player per season, which in economic terms saved the club €1.2 million per season.

Revived DNA offers a similar service to Made of Genes, which works across most sports and many teams but, in the interests of NDAs, can’t say who. Its metric dashboard sucks in genetic, blood and wearables data to generate a dashboard that channels the results into ‘performance’, ‘recovery’ and ‘career longevity’.

Key to the company’s progress is, says founder Mark Notton, understanding the biological pathway: ‘For instance, if you have a blood test and it shows that you’re deficient in vitamin C, you might be prescribed more vitamin C. But the body’s not that simple and it could be a different pathway that’s causing the problem, which might require a different solution. The body isn’t a single root, it’s a massive tree with multiple different pathways.

‘Another example is an athlete who enjoyed an ice bath after exercise, but when we sequenced his genetics we noticed that he naturally had a hard time dilating his blood vessels. That meant by hitting an ice bath, which constricted his vessels further, it impaired recovery and adaptation. He wanted to bulk up, so the team changed the ice bath to hot-water immersion. That helped with the dilation, he adapted better and piled on four pounds of muscle.

‘Then there was the rugby player with 80 caps to his name who, genetically, was the fastest recoverer we’d ever mapped. He said the results matched his experience, as he’d hit training the day after a match and could be ready to play full-on again. He recovered so swiftly his teammates said he had “Wolverine blood”. It’s results like this that make the thought of a digital twin exciting.’

Monitored 24/7

But, in Drawer’s eyes, we’re not there yet: ‘In an ideal world, you’d have embedded sensors tracking the immune system, cardiovascular system, metabolic system… Riders have blood taken every quarter or maybe every eight weeks, but these are just snapshots and you don’t really know what’s happened in between. Constant signals would mean the digital twin would be incredibly accurate and useful.’

Drawer concedes it sounds a little Big Brother, but is it far-fetched? Maybe ten years ago, but riders already use continuous glucose monitors so that Rubicon has already been crossed. ‘Signals from your body would go up to the cloud where your digital twin is sucking in all those signals to tell you to put in a big effort or ease off,’ he says.

Drawer also says the field of digital twins has potential to sprout from the individual to teams. He directs me to Alex Pentland’s book Social Physics, where office workers wore proximity sensors. The field is called ‘sociometry’. The sensors monitored how many times and for how long individuals interacted, be it a chat over the printer or while sipping coffee. ‘They showed the quality of connections among a group was a powerful predictor of a team’s performance, not necessarily in sport but in other domains, but it reflects that we’re social creatures.

‘When you’re racing, you ride as a team, so cohesion and connection is vital. It’s human evolution. It’s how we survived as clans and tribes. That psychosocial connection plays out in physiology. If you bond with someone, believe in someone, you’ll really want to fight for them. That rider would then give that little bit more because they’re more connected to the group. What happens above the neck is untapped. Achieve that with a digital twin and who knows how fast the peloton will ride.’

Ultimately, the future of pro cycling is less about collecting more data and more about understanding what it all means. From Orreco’s AI-powered biomarker analysis to the emerging concept of biological digital twins, technology is bringing teams closer to understanding how riders respond to training, racing and recovery. The goal is not simply to predict when a rider will perform, tire or get injured, but to understand why and what can be done about it. Yet the perfect digital replica remains some way off.

Until continuous biological monitoring becomes a reality, snapshots of bloodwork, wearable data and performance metrics can only tell part of the story. The challenge is turning those fragments into meaningful decisions without losing sight of the human being behind the numbers.

Get that balance right and digital twins could transform talent identification, recovery and race strategy, potentially changing not just how fast cyclists ride, but how long they can sustain their careers. As Drawer suggests, the next frontier may be understanding not only the individual rider, but also the connections that make a team greater than the sum of its parts.

The post What if every rider had a digital clone? The next frontier of scouting, training, racing and recovery using data appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Paul Component Engineering x Sim Works “Sunset” Collection
entry.content:
Paul Component Engineering and Sim Works team up for a limited edition “Sunset” Collection to commemorate the 2026 Bespoked Osaka Framebuilder Showcase, the first edition of the bicycle show to be held in Japan. Read below for all the red and gold details.

Sunset Collection

The “Sunset” Collection is a super limited collection of products built by friends Sim Works and Paul Components in Chico, California. The “Sunset” Collection celebrates the Magical Hour of light that sets in as we approach twilight. A gradient of Red gives way to Orange and Gold. Released to commemorate the inaugural Bespoke Bicycle Show in Osaka Japan, this collection culminates Sim Works’ 2026 limited anodizing offerings and beautifully complements the “Sunrise” collection of parts that we launched at MADE earlier this year in Portland.

The collection includes Paul’s excellent mechanical braking products as a focal point, with both rim and disc brake options in both cable-pull options, as well as their corresponding levers. Distinct, custom elements adorn these parts and set them truly apart from Paul’s standard offerings.

We’ve enjoyed this partnership and their previous collaborative efforts. This collection will serve as a testament to the relationship between an iconic American manufacturer and a beloved Japanese brand.

See the whole collection and more at Sim Works USA.

The post Paul Component Engineering x Sim Works “Sunset” Collection appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 04: Crumbworks, Morralito, Prova, Sim Works, Stayer – John Watson
entry.content:
Maido from Osaka! Cari and John were in attendance at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka event, where they documented a variety of bikes from the global framebuilding community. Read on for a look at the Bespoked Osaka venue and a selection of builders including Crumbworks, Morralito, Prova, Sim Works, and Stayer…

Crumbworks x Farets Bicycles (Big) Chunk

Tokyo-based Crumbworks had a wonderful display at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase featuring a crowd favorite, the Chunk, front and center. The Chunk is made by Farets Bicycles, Crumbworks’ in-house frame company. Owner Keita Matsumoto’s vision for the brand is inspired by vintage cruisers, brands like Crust, and Rivendell. The Chunk is a rigid MTB with clearance for 26 x 2.8″, 27.5 x 2.8″, or 700 x 50 mm tires and lots of standover.

Its tall stack and segmented fork are perhaps overshadowed by the swooping top tube and step-through frame, which still provides enough room for a framebag. The Chunk uses a 1″ steerer, designed for quill stems, allowing for handlebar flex in all the right ways.

Zenzay, the designer of the Chunk and its headbadge was kind enough to pose with his bike, which was a standout at the show. Fitted with custom Hungry bags, they really tie the room together.

Crumbworks Mini Chunk

Teaming up with legendary Japanese builder Osamu Fukuda, who runs Raizin Works, Crumbworks designed a mini velo version of the Chunk, dubbed the Mini Chunk. Designer Zenzay worked closely with Fukuda to ensure the lines and stance of the Mini Chunk were in line with the Big Chunk.

That includes plentiful tire clearance for a cushioned ride, a tall stack height for flat, swept-back Magic Components “KT-800” bars. Fukuda’s fillet brazing is on full display with the Mini Chunk, while the (Big) Chunk is made in Taiwan through Crumbworks’ partners and is TIG-welded. Look out for the Mini Chunk in 2027 from Crumbworks!

Crumbworks owner Keita was there, displaying the new Babylnd Bikes collaboration, launched at Bespoked Osaka. These shirts are available in store at Crumbworks and on Babyldn Bikes’ webshop.

Many thanks to Keita for the thorough explanation of the Crumbworks line and for the hangs!

@Crumbworks

Morralito Inicio Cargo Bike

Mexico City-based Morralito is a collaborative effort between Mario Guzman, Elias Cattan, architects/designers, and Eli “De Bicla” Acosta, a framebuilder. We’ve featured Eli’s work before here on The Radavist thanks to Dani and Karla. Morralito brought the Inicio, an adaptable cargo bike, designed and built for modern city living.

It’s a bike designed around 7 possible builds. You can build it fully mechanical, as shown, or remove the bottom bracket assemblage and install an electric drivetrain. The front box can be removed, and it can be run as a mini velo, or you can swap in a smaller box, a larger box, or you can run it in its long configuration as shown, or a more collapsible/stowable option.

The details and paint design reflect the landscape surrounding Mexico City, with large mountains, and are imbued with the bright, vibrant Mexican culture. When I was given the duty of awarding the best Utility Bike at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase, this was the obvious winner.

It was a real honor to meet all of you and to document your work. Check out the Inicio in detail at Morralito.

@MorralitoBikes

Prova Senza Titanium Full Suspension

Melbourne, Australia-based Prova is all about incremental design. Mark and Kelly Hester, siblings, will create a new model, ride it, and then improve upon it over the years. Case in point is the Senza mountain bike, which I first documented at the 2024 Made Bike Show.

This represents the latest permutation of Prova’s hard work with the Senza. While it still uses the 3V0 suspension layout, Mark has designed Prova’s own swingarm, whereas the first models used the 3Vo-supplied rear end. This has been a slow evolution over the past two years and Mark commented that this new product is so much better and he’s feeling more confident at offering this model as it sits with the new in-house swingarm.

One of the downsides, however, is the time spent welding a Senza. The first prototype only took Mark 40 minutes to build since it relied on an Asia-produced 3Vo CNC aluminum rear end. Now, with the Prova swingarm, the setup and welding time is considerably longer. But Prova’s not about effeciencies, or cutting corners, the team’s one goal is to provide its clients with the best possible product they can offer.

The end result of two years of prototyping is a show-stopper. Well done, Mark and Kelly!

@ProvaCycles

Sim Works Doppo Ronin with Sunrise and Sunset Parts

Nagoya, Japan-based Circles bike shop and its in-house component line Sim Works first launched the Doppo touring bike back in 2016 at NAHBS. Later that year, I was on a bike tour around Japan with Makoto from Sim Works on his Doppo. The brand launched future models, refining and repurposing the Doppo name from touring bikes to mountain bikes, adventure bikes, and fendered road bikes, like the one I documented at the 2026 Made Bike Show.

At the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show, Sim Works unveiled its latest Doppo Ronin model in the Golden Moss colorway. Affixed to the bike were its limited-edition Sunrise edition parts, which include Japan-made Nitto and MKS. The Sunrise pack includes the Beatnik Seatpost, Tomboy Stemcap, Topcap, SimDrop, and the SimWorks by MKS pedal collection. Reaching across the Pacific to Chico, California, the brand then developed the Sunset edition parts. Limited to thirty sets, the Sunset parts include a Paul bottle opener, Short Pull Levers, Klamper disc brakes, and the Motolite V-brakes.

The bike, like Masashi, is incredibly stylish and looks amazing on the Golden Moss Doppo Ronin frame.

@Circles @SimWorks

Stayer Cycles x Sentient Works x Wizard Works Bike of Friendship

London workshop Stayer Cycles debuted what has been referred to as the Bike of Friendship. This mini velo is a 20” full-suspension bike made and styled in collaboration with problem solvers and UK bike makers Sam and Willow from Stayer, Tullen from Sentient Works, Val of Brompton and Blacklinez, and Harry and Ve of Wizard Works.

Mini Velos are great for small apartments or travel. They break down into a smaller bike box, are easier to jetset with, or, in Japan, to rinco on trains. This 20″ BMX trail bike is a collaborative project between Sam from Stayer and Tullen from Sentient, who dressed the frame for the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show in paint by Val and bags from the Wizards. Presented in luggage as a rowdy but prepared travel companion for those looking to shake off the cobwebs after a long haul.

The idea was rooted in asking a single question: how much fun would a full suspension BMX be? From concept to reality, the Bike of Friendship was made possible by many hands, with a special thanks to Hope, Manitou, Brompton, and Schwalbe. Val from Brompton and Vee from Wizard Works developed a flame-adorned Leyline Brompton Bag, and Stayer integrated the Brompton Carrier Block system to the headtube for ease of removal.

Many thanks to Judith from Stayer for the hangs and for bringing the stoke all the way from the UK.

@Stayer @SentientWorks @WizardWorks

Stayer Cycles x Babyldn

Speaking of Stayer, the London-based builders made a travel mini velo for Marlon Plein of BabyLdn. In hopes of making the bike lighter and stiffer in the rear, Sam from Stayer welded up the chain and seat stays from aluminum, which are then bolted to the front triangle of the bike via clevises.

The frame’s truss fork features a unique cable stop integrated into its brace to allow for consistent modulation and control for the cantilever brakes. Marlon’s bike was made possible with parts from MKS, Paul Component, and White Industries.

@Stayer @BabyLdn

The Radavist thanks Circles Japan for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Osaka coverage and our independent Reportage!

The post 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 04: Crumbworks, Morralito, Prova, Sim Works, Stayer appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France Femmes predictions
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France Femmes predictions

How do you follow up a Tour de France Femmes that was heralded as one of the best Grand Tours ever? Maybe a visit to England.

Yes, the 2027 Tour de France Femmes will start in Yorkshire. From Leeds, the race will cross the Pennines twice, back and forth from Manchester to Sheffield before a team time-trial in London. Back in France, the parcours points southwards for stage finishes in Calais, Magnanville and Bourges. The mountains finally arrive on Stage 7 with the race’s first summit finish atop La Loge des Gardes. To round things out, the Massif Central’s most mythical climb, the Puy de Dôme, will host the race’s final mountain test.

So now we know where the next Tour de France Femmes is going, let’s drum up some wildly early predictions and guess who will win the nine stages and four distinctive jerseys next August. Check out my predictions for the men’s race here once you’ve read this one.

Predicting every stage of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes

Stage 1

Ey’ up ar kid. The Tour is coming to Yorkshire and Greater Manchester. Not that the race will spend much time on the roads there, as the opening stage is incredibly short.

The day’s three climbs will seem tough, but they don’t seem to be long enough to shake off the likes of Lorena Wiebes or Marianne Vos. In that case, prepare to see Wiebes roar down Deansgate faster than any of her rivals, yielding a third career stint in the maillot jaune. It’s a no-brainer, really.

Extra prediction incoming. Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be there to hand out the yellow jersey to a very happy Wiebes. We can only hope the two will head to Deansgate Wetherspoons for a recovery Curry Club meal and a cheeky pint afterwards.

Cyclist’s prediction: Lorena Wiebes

Stage 2: Manchester to Sheffield

Stage 2 is more the ticket. It’s a right tough day out in the Pennines, featuring some UK classics like Winnats Pass and Snake Pass.

Now, this is very similar to Stage 2 of the men’s Tour, when that headed to Sheffield in 2014. That day, Jenkin Road ended up being a launchpad for Chris Froome, Vincenzo Nibali and Alberto Contador to show face on a rather mundane Yorkshire road.

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney won’t be able to resist the urge to attack there, and we suddenly have a real GC battle on our hands. Demi Vollering, Paula Blasi and Elisa Longo Borghini follow and the group manage to hold a gap to the end. It’s a sprint between them for the stage win, claimed by the newly-crowned world champion Vollering.

Feeling groggy after her microwave jalfrezi, Wiebes hands yellow over to Vollering as a result of the stage win.

Cyclist’s prediction: Demi Vollering

Stage 3

In London, the women will be treated to the kind of sightseeing tour that’s usually only handed to those who fork £200 on a fluffy rickshaw. We’ve got Big Ben, Tower Bridge, Hyde Park, Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace all squeezed into an 18km loop.

While that’ll guarantee good TV shots, it’s unknown how the stage will pan out. We don’t have many team time-trials on the women’s circuit, so it’s hard to judge team performance. I reckon that’ll motivate a few to get in the wind tunnel this off-season, given that this will be the only race against the clock at the 2027 edition.

Lidl-Trek, Visma-Lease a Bike and FDJ United-Suez could all be candidates for victory, but I’m backing SD Worx-Protime.

In a roster that includes Anna van der Breggen, Lotte Kopecky, Misha Bredewold, Lorena Wiebes and new recruit Cédrine Kerbaol, it seems as though SD Worx have the strength on paper to pull this one off.

Cyclist’s prediction: SD Worx-Protime

Stage 4

We finally make it back to France after our three-day trip to England. And once the Eurotunnel is conquered, the riders will be back on rolling roads, this time over the white cliffs of Calais.

The coast is very exposed to the wind, so an attack on the Cap Blanc-Nez would require some confidence because a 12km solo in harsh winds will be tough to pull off.

There’s no need for Vollering to roll the dice, nor Niewidaoma-Phinney to make a move, given what’s to come the following afternoon. It’s the kind of thing prime Lotte Kopecky could do. However, we don’t have prime Kopecky anymore and Lorena Wiebes seems to be ever more comfortable on the climbs these days.

Boring.

Cyclist’s prediction: Lorena Wiebes

Stage 5

Time for another Classics-like stage. This time, it heads into the Vexin, a part of France that rarely gets the chance to host the Tour, thanks to its close proximity to the French capital.

That’s a shame, because this stage looks like a banger, with at least six categorised climbs in the final 50km. A few of them will offer double-digit gradients, so expect a more Liège-Bastogne-Liège kind of finale than what we had in Calais the previous day.

Fans of cheese will recognise Magnanville as the host town of Paris-Camembert, although the Paris end rather than the cheesy finale. The Côte de Magnanville has appeared a few times at Paris-Nice. It’s 1km long and at an average of 5%, so it’ll be a bit of a drag for the sprinters in the final kilometre of this stage.

It seems blindlingly obvious to pick Kim Le Court-Pienaar in that case. She’s won stages like this at both the 2025 and 2026 editions, and she’s a winner of Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

It’s starting to feel like groundhog day, isn’t it?

Cyclist’s prediction: Kim Le Court-Pienaar

Stage 6

On paper, this is the most conventional sprint stage of the week.

However, there is one sprinter miles ahead of everyone right now. That’s Lorena Wiebes.

She’ll win by a few bike lengths, so she’ll have some time to come up with a showstopping celebration. Something inspired by local hero Joan of Arc? Another two-headed Albanian eagle? A gang sign or a gesture making refernce to her team’s HR platform sponsor?

Cyclist’s prediction: Lorena Wiebes

Stage 7

I guess this will be our first mountain stage of the race, despite some people’s claims that La Loge des Gardes isn’t a proper summit finish.

Fair enough, it isn’t the steepest climb out there. It barely goes above 8%, so it’s really a climb for the engines. That indicates that it won’t be too attritional for the big GC favourites. History concurs. This has been used twice at recent editions of Paris-Nice and the winner has never come home solo.

Chances are, Vollering would still win a four-up sprint atop the mountain, meaning she strengthens her grip on the overall lead. The gaps will be slim, but it’ll distill the fight for the podium down to just a few names.

I say that, but here’s to hoping Paula Blasi makes the difference and bags her first ever Tour stage atop the Loge.

Cyclist’s prediction: Demi Vollering

Stage 8

At this point in the race, we are knee-deep in the Massif Central. As such, Marion Rousse has designed a stage that heads over every bump on offer in this volcanic highland.

This is the perfect day to sweep up QOM points, so I believe this will be fought out among the breakaway. I can envision the likes of Puck Pieterse, Magdeleine Vallieres and Célia Gery heading up the road, but it all depends on whether they play out the GC or not.

The Côte de Charade will filter the GC group down somewhat, but I feel the riders will be waiting to lay down the gauntlet on the Puy de Dôme. Then again, a few time gaps didn’t hurt anyone.

Cyclist’s prediction: Puck Pieterse

Stage 9

First of all, forgive the above image, because there won’t be any fans on Puy de Dôme. OK, that’s not confirmed yet, but its conservation status has restricted fans in the past, so expect a quiet arrival atop the Massif Central’s most iconic mountain.

Now, the final mountain stage of the Tour de France Femmes has never gone to an escapee. Expect the same to happen here, leaving the likes of Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney to fight out the stage and possibly the GC.

Puy de Dôme’s final kilometres are fiendishly steep, so I’m inclined to favour Niewidoma-Phinney on an arrival like this. She proved on Mont Ventoux this year that she’s more of a specialist on longer uphill finishes, and I feel she’ll be motivated to get something out of this race given Vollering will have led the GC quite comfortably up until now.

Saying that, the World Champ does enough to limit her losses in order to retain the yellow jersey for another year.

Cyclist’s prediction: Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney

The GC podium and jersey predictions

Unsurprisingly, I think Demi Vollering will be able to pull on the yellow jersey once again, making her the first rider to win this event on three occasions. She’s gone undefeated in 2026 and it just feels as though she’s hitting her prime.

As for the remainder of the podium, I have Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Paula Blasi written down. Niewiadoma-Phinney will relish the final stage, but Blasi seems like a burgeoning GC all-rounder, possibly with a domestique-de-luxe in Marlen Reusser at her disposal.

By virtue of her three stage victories, Lorena Wiebes will comfortably win another green jersey. As for the white jersey, we can only guess because the Tour organisers keep changing the rules. However, I’ll go out on a confident whim and say Puck Pieterse doubles up on polka-dot jerseys after her success at this year’s race.

It’s 2026 all over again.

The post Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France Femmes predictions appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: San Util Design’s Updated Whirlpool MkII
entry.content:
The San Util Design Whirlpool MkII is an updated version of their classic hip pack, a utilitarian gear-hauler. The MkII refresh gets more pockets, more organization, and more whirlpool. But don’t worry, the simpler “classic” design is still on offer. You don’t have to have the fancy stuff unless you really want it.

The Whirlpool MkII is an evolution of San Util’s classic gear-hauling hip pack. The Whirlpool MkII builds on the design elements that made the original Whirlpool so good. The classic version was a simple bag that carries weight well, can be overstuffed, and is perfect for a bladder. The MkII adds some big zippered pockets on the wings, a dedicated phone pocket on the back, and more internal organization.

If you wanted more swirl to your whirlpool, this answers your desires.

San Util Whirlpool MkII Design Overview

San Util uses a 420D face fabric laminated with an X-ply and 70D internal layer. A 200D Oxford Packcloth makes it easy to see inside the bag and adds more abrasion resistance. All the buckles are high-quality Woojin, Duraflex, and Fidlock buckles for quick access and durability.

If you are a fan of the classic Whirlpool, don’t worry, it’s not going anywhere. You’ll find it in the San Util catalog, solidified in its place with a “classic” moniker. The classic and updated versions share these fundamental features:

  • Designed around a 1.5L lumbar bladder (sold separately)
  • Works with our bottle holsters for more water carrying capacity
  • Utility daisy chain for lashing extra gear
  • Compression straps on bottom for rain jacket or knee pads
  • Roll-top and expandable
  • Visible orange liner fabric

Whirlpool MkII Updates

  • Slightly larger volume (roughly 4L – 6L)
  • Large wing zipper pockets w/ key loop
  • Spine column on back for added stability
  • Same floating wing design as the “classic” (we are still selling our original Whirlpool and calling it the Classic)
  • Internal zipper pocket, drop pockets and bladder sleeve
  • External phone pocket for easy access
  • Fabric: 420D laminated sailcloth with a 70D backer
  • Liner: 200D Oxford Pack Cloth
  • Buckles: Woojin, Duraflex, Fidlock
  • Weight: 471g
  • Cost: $135

See the Whirlpool MkII and more at San Util.
