entry.title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 03: Aya, Blue Lug, Cook Paint Works, Cicli Barco – John Watson
entry.content:
Maido from Osaka! Cari and John were in attendance at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka event, where they documented a variety of bikes from the global framebuilding community. Read on for a look at the Bespoked Osaka venue and a selection of builders including Aya Bikes, Blue Lug, Cook Paint Works, and Cicli Barco…

Aya Bikes Ghooost ATB

Himeji City-based Aya Akamatsu learned to build frames at the Tokyo College of Cycle Design; three years later, she began building the Sim Works Doppo frames for four years. At the 2026 Bespoked Osaka event, she unveiled Mai Ohara from Ghooost’s new bike.

Aya wanted to make a frame for shorter Japanese people, particularly women, and Mai was the perfect client for this first bike. The average ATB or gravel bike on the market is often too big for Japanese women, so Aya worked on perfecting the size and proportions of the frame for Mai. Some beautiful details are found throughout, including reinforcement rings of brass, which are perforated with small holes that were inspired by Mai’s artwork.

Once the frame was complete, Aya had one last thing to do: build a stem for it. After that, the bike was complete. For the Bespoked show, Mai put on the finishing touches with her playful illustrations and creatures, including a special note for Jonny Pucci to come paint the bike in Japan.

Mai, Aya, and their friend V, an English interpreter, were super busy all weekend at Bespoked. We’re big fans of Ghooost over here and can’t wait to see Mai ride this bike all over the globe.

@AyaBikes

Blue Lug x Toyo x Falconer Pro Cruiser Homage “Chukar”

Walking into one of the two Bespoked Osaka halls, my vintage MTB-loving eyes were immediately drawn to this Pro Cruiser homage on display at the Blue Lug booth. Little did I know that Cameron Falconer – who has actually stepped aside from his framebuilding business recently – didn’t actually build the bike. Rather, when Tani from Blue Lug approached Cam to build a frame, he gladly handed over the drawings to Japanese builder Mr. Ishigaki from Toyo.

Left, Mr. Ishigaki is shown with a special Japan-built Rivendell he also made for Blue Lug for a small batch coming out in 2027… Champion BMX downtube piercing, right.

Toyo has been building bikes since the 1980s and was actually one of the first Japanese builders to make mountain bikes for various brands, including the first Specialized Stumpjumpers. After Mike Sinyard from Specialized bought a Ritchey frame and shipped it to Japan to be copied, Toyo delivered the brand’s first mountain bike.

Needless to say, Toyo was the perfect company to build this bike. He even went as far as to pierce the downtube with the diagatube, just as Champion BMX had done so in the original design the Pro Cruiser was inspired by.

Blue Lug will be producing these bikes in a small batch next year, and I cannot wait. To the whole team at Blue Lug. Thank you!

@BlueLug

Cook Paint Works x Ron’s Bikes

Blue Lug’s in-house paint shop, Cook Paint Works, recently collaborated with San Diego artist and bicycle painter Jonny Pucci on a limited run of Ron’s Bikes frames. We reported on that collaboration earlier this year. Following that momentum, Konno-boy from Cook looked around the Blue Lug shop at various sewn goods for inspiration to paint two more frames.

The Darren Larkin-built steel CR1 long-reach caliper road bike was painted to resemble a tie-dye seat cushion Konno uses while working, while the Frank the Welder-built Alumax II was painted with a “Night Tree Camo” pattern—a design featured on the Shtak messenger bags made by Jag that Konno uses.

The Cook logo on the Alumax II was made with gold leafing, a special touch Konno will add to his most favorite projects, upping the ante for the Bespoked Osaka showcase.

To the entire Blue Lug crew, arigato gozaimasu!

@CookPaintWorks @RonsBikes

Cicli Barco Viva Integrated Disc Road

Fitting hydraulic brake lines into a 1 1/8″ cockpit was no easy task for Piazzola sul Brenta, Italy-based Cicli Barco. The Italian builder dropped the mic on modern steel road bikes using obtuse carbon forks for integrated cockpits, proving it is, in fact, a certain possibility for more traditional lines and proportions.

Gianluca Barco walked me through the process it took to cram brake hoses into the Ritchey bars, through the stem and into the head tube. When I requested photos of the spaghetti, he winced, noting that getting it all into the frame takes time and patience. Perhaps we’ll see more some other day.

This stainless steel beauty has nods to the Cicli Barco heritage as an Italian manufacturer for bigger brands throughout the decades. Featured throughout is a “B” from the Barco namesake, hidden on the underside of the stem, on the ends of the custom-made titanium thru-axles, dropouts, and bottom bracket.

The stem’s compression slit is off-center; the fastback seat cluster uses titanium hardware, and the elegant stainless steel fork balances the proportions with an elegance only the Italians can showcase. This bike was hands down both Petor Georgallou, the Bespoked owner and director, and my own favorite road bike at the show. It embodies the blending of classic Italian heritage with modern demands, in a package that is both traditional and innovative.

Gianluca, it was a pleasure and an honor to document your work.

@CicliBarco

 

The Radavist thanks Circles Japan for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Osaka coverage and our independent Reportage!

The post 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 03: Aya, Blue Lug, Cook Paint Works, Cicli Barco appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka Showcase: 大阪 – John Watson
entry.content:
In line with our Beautiful Bicycle Reportage from the 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase, we’ve got a gallery jam-packed with images of Osaka and the show itself by John…

Coming off my second Bespoked showcase this year and my third framebuilding show, I was eagerly awaiting to walk through the halls of the Glion Museum.

Knowing the Japanese people’s fondness for traditional bicycle forms, I was expecting a number of quill stems and classic randonneuring bikes, mixed in with a younger generation’s take on modern ATB and tourers.

The show did not disappoint. Petor Georgallou’s vision for a Bespoked based in Japan was on full display, mixing traditional companies like MKS, Nitto, and Honjo, alongside pinnacle shops like Circles and Blue Lug, as well as framebuilders from all generations. Welcomed were Asia-Pacific builders like D3 and Prova, as well as a number of European talents.

Bespoked has always felt global, but Osaka brought a regional specificity. Osaka’s vibes as a city are much more laid-back and slower-paced than Tokyo, with local dining, shopping, and entertainment just a short subway trip away.

The city is beautiful, expansive, and vibrant, which made for a relaxing experience post-showcase each night.

My takeaway from the event is a newfound reverence for Japanese builders, seeing many in person for the first time, as well as the utmost respect for brands like Cherubim who’ve spent decades wowing framebuilder showcase attendees. Seeing them on their home turf was even more special.

To the readers of The Radavist and longtime fans from the Prolly is Not Probably days that stopped me and said hello, I appreciate you. A special shout-out to the Circles and Sim Works fam; thank you for making this trip possible. Much love for the Blue Lug posse, who brought energy and one sick employee bike parking show in itself. Thanks to the Crumbworks team for keeping it fun!

I really also want to thank our readership for clicking into these articles, commenting, sharing the posts on social media, and all the global chatter you create around this funky little corner of the internet. This has been my life’s work, and I couldn’t be more proud to call it home with all of you.

The Japanese concept of ikigai – 生きがい – “reason for being” is on display at this show. While not intrinsically linked to being profit-driven, your ikigai can be derived from asking four questions: What are you good at? What do you love? What does the world need? And what can you be paid for? This concept lies at the root of artistic pursuit, a passion for creation, and the drive to fill a needed niche in society. For me, my ikigai is documenting the work of makers, largely in this cycling space and I feel so fulfilled documenting shows like Bespoked.

Many thanks to the people of Japan (and beyond) and the host city of Osaka for showing up. I can’t wait to return next year.

 

The Radavist thanks Circles Japan for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Osaka coverage and our independent Reportage!

entry.title: Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France 2027 predictions
entry.content:
Cyclist
Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France 2027 predictions

We’ve now had a few days to digest the 2027 Tour de France route.

Revealed in Paris last week, the parcours has stirred up some strong opinions. Most of this has been attributed to the 71km of time-trialling, the longest used at a Tour since 2012, and the small number of mountaintop finishes. In fact, there are just three, coming at the Grand Colombier, Les Saisies and the Col du Portet.

Now we know where the Tour de France is going next year, it’s time to reach for the crystal ball. In this wildly early list of prognostics, we’ll predict how each of the 21 stages will go, plus who will be the winner of all four jerseys and the final GC podium. Before you read on, check out how I got on in last year’s way-too-early Tour predictions.

Who’s going to be racing the Tour de France 2027?

Time to make our first punts, because only a handful of riders have explicitly said that they’ll be on the start line in Edinburgh next July.

Among those confirmed is Tadej Pogačar, who revealed a busy racing 2027 programme last week. His big goals will be the Tour de France and World Championships, which come straight after in the French Alps.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe have insinuated that Remco Evenepoel will be there in Scotland next July. That’s hardly a surprise, given this parcours is said to be the most Evenepoel-friendly in years. Jonas Vingegaard is also expected to make his return after crashing out in the Alps last summer. Wout van Aert is likely to be on the roster, but Britain’s Matt Brennan’s inclusion is TBC for now, even after his five stage victories at the Vuelta this autumn.

Paul Seixas has sent out mixed signals this week after appearing on a French podcast, on which he suggested that the Tour isn’t certain for his 2027 schedule, while Italian newspaper Gazzetta dello Sport suggests that Seixas could be one of a few top-name riders to pick the Giro in 2027. Among them is Isaac de Toro, who sailed onto the podium on Tour debut ahead of Seixas.

In terms of sprinters, it’s a little more hazy. Tim Merlier is almost guaranteed after his comments at last week’s route presentation, 2025 green jersey winner Jonathan Milan has been tipped for a Tour comeback, and 2023 green jersey winner Jasper Philipsen seems a shoo-in for the 2027 race. However, it’s unclear whether Decathlon CMA CGM will send stage winner Olav Kooij to the Tour after Seixas proved his leader status last year.

Stage 1

Who’d have thought that Carlisle would end up being the most pivotal place on the sprinting map in 2027?

Yes, the Cumbrian town once home to the world’s largest stained glass window will soon be the centre of the sprinting universe as it welcomes the finish of Stage 1. With little elevation south of Midlothian, the sprinters have been handed a real chance of getting to battle for the race’s first yellow jersey.

There are always a few hiccups on a Tour’s opening stage. Think Opi-Omi, the GreenEdge bus getting stuck, the informal neutralisation in Nice and Mark Cavendish’s crash in front of PM David Cameron. Something is bound to go wrong, so a scrappy sprint is likely.

Cyclist’s prediction: Olav Kooij

Stage 2

After a night’s rest and a hefty fry-up in Cumbria, the peloton’s nerves will no doubt be settled

I’ve heard from those who’ve recced the route that the section through the Lancashire hills is more demanding than expected. That could catch a few out, but I reckon everything will come together by the time the race enters Liverpool and sprints down the Strand, right by the statues dedicated to the city’s Fab Four.

If you couldn’t tell then, I reckon this is a paint-by-numbers sprint.

Call up the Belgians because I predict a battle between Tim Merlier and Jasper Philipsen. In recent years, Merlier has looked the stronger of the two.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tim Merlier

Stage 3

Wales will be the scene of the race’s first real test, and Christian Prudhomme has been quite excited about the prospect of an early GC battle in the valleys of South Wales.

However, the bulk of the stage’s real tough climbs come a long way out from the finish line in what will be a very long day out. Sure, this could produce a Liège-Bastogne-Liège kind of scenario, but it’s had to replicate a one-day race in an event spanning three weeks, especially when everyone is fresh and up for the fight.

That said, it’s hard to tell whether this will end up resembling a Classic or more a reduced bunch sprint. Caerphilly Mountain has a mixed hit rate at grounding the peloton down at the Tour of Britain, so it might act as more of a filter than a launch pad.

In that case, it’ll be someone who can sprint well after a few hills. Cue our first Van der Poel vs Van Aert battle of the 2027 race.

Cyclist’s prediction: Wout van Aert

Stage 4

After boking in a paper bag aboard a P&O ferry, the peloton will return to France after a rest day in Normandy.

Wind could be an issue here on what could be a deceptively bumpy arrival. On a false-flat finish like this, you’d like to pick Mads Pedersen, but the Dane’s participation isn’t guaranteed for the moment.

This could really go the way of any tough sprinter. Hey, it could even go to Tadej Pogačar. Crazier things have happened.

Cyclist’s prediction: Anthony Turgis

Stage 5

The Côte de Cadoudal is getting a bit overshadowed in all the parcours discourse, but this is a staple of Breton cycling. It has featured in the Tour de France on several occasions, welcomed the European Road Championships and hosts Coupe de France one-day races every year. In fact, this is the only hill outside the Alps, Vosges or Pyrenees to host both a Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes stage finish.

The climb will be tackled on two occasions during the final 15km to guarantee splits.

When the women visited in 2025, the top ten was split between GC contenders, hardy sprinters and Classics specialists. I suspect it’ll be similar when the men arrive next July. However, given the likeness to the nearby Mûr-de-Bretagne, I’m going to back Mathieu van der Poel, who won atop that climb back in 2021.

Cyclist’s prediction: Mathieu van der Poel

Stage 6

This is quite possibly the most generic sprint stage you could find.

The nerves of the first few days would have settled and there’s a near-zero chance the breakaway goes all the way. There’s even the chance that no rider even bothers to go up the road.

It’ll be up to the best sprinters in the game to fight it out between them, and I believe Merlier is the top dog right now.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tim Merlier

Stage 7

We’ve not had an ITT as long as this in the Tour’s opening week since the days of Armstrong, Ullrich and blood transfusions.

This 38km stage is as flat as a syringe needle. There aren’t any major obstacles, so it really should favour the specialists, four-time world champ Remco Evenepoel for example.

Maybe Pippo Ganna’s new Trek rig will be help him break Remco’s stranglehold on this discipline. Similarly, a storm could be afoot once the rainbow jersey rolls off, handing early starters a bit of an advantage. Who knows?

But what I do know is that Evenepoel is the world’s best time-trialist – no question about it. He’ll take the stage and presumably the yellow jersey with it unless a breakaway manages to gain a handful of time in Wales or Normandy.

Cyclist’s prediction: Remco Evenepoel

Stage 8

With Evenepoel now in yellow, the race has settled down. That’ll give the breakaway the ideal opportunity to go out in search of their first big chance in this Tour de France.

This region, the Morvan, last hosted a stage in 2021, on a profile similar in both topography and length. On that occasion, the breakaway made it all the way to the end, with Matej Mohorič victorious.

I reckon the same will happen in 2027, but with another breakaway expert victorious. Quinn Simmons deserves a Grand Tour stage win at some point soon, but Ben Healy seems to roll out of his cave every two years. He thrives in years with odd numbers, and I reckon EF will be hungry for a stage win at their first Tour without Richard Carapaz.

Cyclist’s prediction: Ben Healy

Stage 9

After moving east through metropolitan France, the peloton will meet their first serious mountains on Stage 9.

Now, the Tour’s opening mountain stage hasn’t gone the way of a breakaway since 2023, and even then the break included Felix Gall and Jai Hindley. History therefore dictates that the peloton will work towards winning this stage. Remember: teams will be fired up to unleash some wrath in the mountains, and everyone will be alert and feeling fresher than ever.

In that sense, we’ll get our first questions answered. Some expected names will drop down the standings, but a group of around ten or so will be there to contest the stage win during the final kilometre. It’ll be up to whoever has the best kick, but that seems to be Tadej Pogačar on paper.

Incredibly, this would therefore be Pogačar’s first stage victory in trade team colours since the beginning of the 2024 edition and somehow just his second ever.

I’ll be honest, the Grand Colombier hasn’t been a particularly decisive climb in recent Tours. I suspect gaps will be small over the top and Evenepoel remains in yellow.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tadej Pogačar

Stage 10

If you’re looking for a stage where Pogačar gains three minutes, this is the one.

How so? Well, I reckon he’ll lift off on the Plateau d’Assy after his team put on the pressure over the previous climbs. The Slovenian is likely to know Domancy like the back of his hand, given he’ll be hungry to win the rainbow jersey when the climb takes centre stage a month later. Cresting that peak solo, he’ll have done enough to put himself in the overall lead, reversing the losses in week one’s time-trial.

All of a sudden, the Tour will start to feel a lot more familiar.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tadej Pogačar

Stage 11

After the Pogcineration, Stage 11 will be a lot tamer as the GC wound-licking begins.

The early position of the Colombière and Croix Fry climbs suggests there will be a fierce battle for the breakaway. Furthermore, the big gap between the opening climbs and the final pair of hors catégorie tests gives me the idea that the peloton will sit up and try to regroup before the stage’s final sequence.

Since this one is going the way of the breakaway, we’ll begin to see who the real candidates are for the polka-dot jersey. I suspect they’ll be a mix of GC guys who ran into trouble in Wales, or those who are allergic to an aero TT position. So, Cian Uijtdebroeks, Lenny Martinez and Santiago Buitrago, your time has come.

In the group of favourites, Pogačar will spring off the front on the final climb, with Vingegaard in pursuit and Evenepoel dangling somewhere further behind. This’ll open up a fierce GC battle between the Dane and the Belgian, which is set to rumble on throughout this Tour.

Cyclist’s prediction: Lenny Martinez

Stage 12

We could have had an Alpine stage here, but we dodge every col possible in favour of heading to the fringes of Provence.

Valence has hosted many a sprint stage over the past decade or so. Last time, it was Jonathan Milan, but the honours this time will be passed to Jasper Philipsen, who often manages to weather the mountains better than most sprinters.

Cyclist’s prediction: Jasper Philipsen

Stage 13

We continue the sprinting theme as the riders tackle what will be the flattest day since Stage 6. You’d think this would make it easy, as this looks like the most humdrum transitional stage ever, but this part of the world can be pretty windy.

in fact, the final part of this stage will be wholly exposed to the elements. The crosswinds will strike, and some fast men and GC guys will be caught out.

As the kings of crosswinds, Soudal Quick-Step (which by then will be Soudal Safety Jogger) will pile on the pressure and deliver Tim Merlier to yet another stage victory.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tim Merlier

Stage 14

Christian Prudhomme has been on record saying that Stage 14 is his favourite of the Tour. I’m inclined to agree with him, as I have no idea how this is going to pan out.

The 4,000m of elevation gain suggests that this could be really quite attritional, although none of the climbs are real blockbuster names. However, these lesser-known central mountains have often been underestimated, leading to quite exciting racing.

That said, I think this will go the way of a breakaway, but only just.

Expect a fierce battle at both ends of the race: the breakaway and the peloton. As for the escapees, the group will be filled with riders trying to flip their fortunes around in this Tour de France.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tobias Halland Johannessen

Stage 15

One for the sprinters or one for the breakaway? This stage could really go either way.

However, my sample of similar stages at the end of week two often favours the breakaway. In that case, this’ll be one for the rouleurs and those with real racing mindsets. An attack at the right time would lead to victory, but who would have the engine necessary to pick up the win?

People like Jasper Stuyven, Victor Campenaerts and Mathias Vacek could be up there. However, with Pogačar in yellow, UAE Team Emirates XRG allow Florian Vermeersch a bit of fun and the chance for him to search out a career-first Grand Tour stage win.

Cyclist’s prediction: Florian Vermeersch

Stage 16

The second dose of time-trialling comes in Toulouse, a city that has been on the TdF map since the race started in 1903.

Nevertheless, a time-trial feels like a foregone conclusion in modern racing. Of course, this should be one for Remco Evenepoel, despite the strategic placement of a steep ramp toward the end of the stage. If I were to guess, I reckon the Belgian takes between 30 and 40 seconds on the stage, which won’t be enough to reclaim yellow, but will be enough to have us believe that there’s still some hope for someone to challenge Pogačar during the final mountain stages.

Cyclist’s prediction: Remco Evenepoel

Stage 17

You hear about stages for the ages, but this is the complete opposite. It’s a sprint stage that I really couldn’t care less about. To add to the boredom, it ends in a place we’ve visited all too often in the Tour: Pau.

That said, this might end up being the last chance for the sprinters at the 2027 race. I reckon Tim Merlier will have abandoned by this point – he has a habit of this – but Jasper Philipsen will no doubt be here. He hasn’t gone home from a Tour empty-handed since 2021.

Thank God this is on a Wednesday. That gives an excuse to skip watching this one live.

Cyclist’s prediction: Jasper Philipsen

Stage 18

Time for the queen stage, and the lowest-altitude Souvenir Henri Desgrange in over a decade.

That’s beside the point, this stage is still poised for a big GC battle. The relentless trail of mountains should favour the mountain train of UAE Team Emirates XRG, who will tee Pogačar up for a real exhibition on the Col du Portet. He’s won there before, and he’ll be hoping to place a final nail in the GC coffin after losing some time to Evenepoel in the Toulouse time-trial.

If there was a stage that will threaten Evenepoel, this could be it. High altitude, back-to-back mountains. This stage will heat up that duel between himself and Vingegaard for the second-place spot.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tadej Pogačar

Stage 19

Again, the race will feel somewhat deflated, but the show must go on. It’s the final mountain stage after all, and we can expect at least one GC contender to find themself spat out far too early on this stage. It’s a tale as old as time.

The GC will be left feeling cagey, as riders rest upon their laurels and hope to consolidate their places in the top ten.

In that case, this will surely be a last hurrah for the breakaway. It’ll be a good chance to get polka-dot jersey points, but I reckon the stage honours will go to a rider who looked set for a top ten before an off-day through them out of contention. It’s hard to forecast that, but Oscar Onley’s name springs to mind.

Cyclist’s prediction: Oscar Onley

Stage 20

This is an absolute snooze fest of a stage, I’ll tell you that for free. It’s not particularly windy in this part of France, and it doesn’t exactly offer you the kind of scenic spots that’ll have you itching to go on Airbnb.

With everyone essentially clocked off, and half the sprinting field absent, the breakaway will be handed a final bone. At least, that’s what happened when Libourne last hosted a Tour stage in 2021.

Copy and paste what I said about the stage to Albi. Except, I think this stage will entice some of the second-tier sprinters who have missed out on a chance of stage glory. The Mads Pedersen, Biniam Girmay or even Davide Ballerini type. It’ll require some Classics legs to break free and read the situation.

Cyclist’s prediction: Davide Ballerini

Stage 21

I wish terrible returns for whoever tried to peddle the rumour that the Tour would be ditching Montmartre in 2027. After the stinker on Stage 20, that would have been a real travesty for all involved.

Alas. Cinderella, we will go to the ball because Montmartre is back for another year.

This Classics-like circuit has produced A-list victories since its introduction. There was Wout van Aert, then Mathieu van der Poel last July. You could even include Remco Evenepoel on that list, as he won Olympic gold on a similar course.

That suggests only someone within that elite ring has the capability to win on this loop, and after trying his damn hardest in 2025 and 2026, I reckon 2027 is the turn of Tadej Pogačar. His form will begin to spike again in preparation for the Worlds, and he’ll be able to distance a tired Van der Poel on the final ascent up Rue Lepic.

And like that, the Slovenian will win a record-breaking sixth Tour and become the first Tour champion to win in Paris since 1982.

Cyclist’s prediction: Tadej Pogačar

The GC podium and jersey predictions

I spoiled it there, but I am backing Pogačar to win a sixth Tour de France. Despite tabling a route that looks as Pog-proof as it can be, the Slovenian is just too strong to let a time-trial get in the way of another Tour victory. As for second, I think Remco Evenepoel will be able to pip Jonas Vingegaard, having gained a big buffer over the Dane against the clock.

That would mean we won’t have the white jersey on the final podium for the first time since 2018. I reckon Paul Seixas will miss out on the final podium again, but a white jersey will prove a consolation prize for a rider still finding his feet at Grand Tours.

The green jersey will return to a traditional sprinter in 2026 in my eyes. Tim Merlier never goes for the points classification, so I guess I have to back Jasper Philipsen for that prize, having won two stages in my predictions. As for polka-dots, I’m leaning toward Lenny Martinez. This parcours does not suit his GC strengths, so a breakaway run like 2025 seems very likely.

The post Cyclist’s way-too-early Tour de France 2027 predictions appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Selwyn Bicycles Wants You To Pick up Your Trail Bike in the French Alps
entry.content:
John documented the Selwyn Bicycles Trail Bike (€8,850 complete) at this year’s Bespoked London event, and today, the French Alps-based builder has opened up orders…

After three years of building, riding and testing in the French Alps. The Selwyn Bicycles Trail Bike is ready.

Alexander Plaisted has been building custom steel frames since 2016, out of a workshop in Samoëns, Haute-Savoie, in the French Alps. The Trail Bike is the result of three years of engineering, prototyping and testing. It is a full-suspension steel mountain bike designed to ride all day, all over the Alps. To take on multi-day point to point mountain adventures. For long days pedalling, pushing and carrying to access high alpine technical trails. For summer lift laps and winter training missions.

Why This Bike

Selwyn partnered with Dan Roberts of Garage Bike Project to build something unique. Together, they’ve created a unique machine. A frame designed and made by hand in the Alps. Traditional brazing skills combined with modern manufacturing processes. A suspension layout that just works in every situation.

Every bike is collected in person from my workshop in Samoëns, where Alexander will take you out on the trails the bike was designed for. The workshop sits in the woods of the Giffre valley, hidden between Morzine and Chamonix, near the start of the mythical Col de Joux Plane road climb. At the bottom of 1,000 vertical metres of singletrack heaven. The small workshop doesn’t offer delivery. That is the point.

Trail Bike Specs

140 mm of rear travel paired with 160 mm up front via a Horst link layout. 140 mm is the magic number for a true alpine bike, enough to handle the most technical terrain while remaining sharp and efficient under pedaling. 29-inch wheels throughout. No mullet option. No 160/160 version. No 170 fork. Every design decision was taken on the basis of whether or not it improves the way the bike rides, and three years of development says it is spot on as it is.

The frame is built from a specific combination of Reynolds 853, 631, and 931 tubing. Every pivot bolt, axle, spacer, dropout, and brake mount is designed by us. Nothing is off the shelf. The dropouts, chainstay yoke and seat stay pivots are 3D printed in stainless steel. The rocker link and all pivot hardware are machined from 7075 aluminum, anodized and engraved with the Selwyn logo.

Availability and Pricing

The house special build runs a custom-tuned FAST Fenix 2 coil shock, tuned specifically for each rider’s weight before the frame leaves the workshop, alongside a RockShox Lyrik Ultimate fork, Hope wheels, brakes and cockpit, and SRAM Eagle 90 Transmission. Every Hope component is available in your choice of color.

Wet paint is standard in Metallic British Racing Green with yellow logos or Pearl Blue with silver logos. Full custom paint available on request.

The Trail Bike is available to order now at selwynbicycles.co.uk. Full build pricing starts at €8,850. Frame-only pricing is available on request. Every order begins with a conversation.

entry.title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 02: Alps, BTCHN, Cherubim, Curve, Yanagi – John Watson
entry.content:
Maido from Osaka! Cari and John were in attendance at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka event, where they documented a variety of bikes from the global framebuilding community. Read on for a look at the Bespoked Osaka venue and a selection of builders including Alps, BTCHN, Cherubim, Curve, and Yanagi…

Alps Climber Ti

Hiroshi Hagiwara founded the Japanese brand Sports Cycle Alps, and it closed 19 years ago. Hitoshi Omae recently relaunched the brand and to commemorate the relaunch, Hitoshi pinged Japanese framebuilder Moriai to build a titanium frameset, designed to mimic the lines of a traditional steel bike.

Mated with a steel fork, which Atelier Kinopio painted closely to match the color of the frame, the Alps Climber Ti planes and flexes while weighing a scant 8.7kg, including the Kimura Manufacturing Co flashlight.

The bike features special chainrings, designed for the TA cranks and 10-speed chains, and features a 25-tooth inner ring, which, if you are a fan of TA cranks, you’ll know usually only go to 26 teeth. If you’re interested in buying a complete bike as shown, it’ll set ya back a cool 1,100,000 yen, or around $ 7,000 USD.

@VeloApres

BTCHN 32er Lefty

Tyler Reiswig, owner and builder at Chico, California’s BTCHN Bikes, rarely leaves his home in Butte County. This trip was his first time traveling internationally. When Silca offered to take him to Japan for Bespoked, he built up a wild 32er hardtail, paired with a Lefty fork and some handlebars that sparked lively conversations all weekend at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show.

While they look obtuse with four brake levers, there is some methodology to the madness, Tyler explained. Typically, when you’re in aero bars, you lack brake levers, so Tyler mated the brake lines for the XT and GRX brakes and added blips to shift the derailleur, on top of a normal AXS shifter.

His decision to choose a Lefty fork came from a quest for stiffness. Other forks he’d used were too noodly and twisted unreasonably. The lefty was not only the stiffest option out there, but also the lightest. Tyler machined a volume spacer to adapt it to the 32er wheelsize and Berd built him custom wheels for the Lefty hub.

Combing through the bike’s details in and out of post typhoon light rain showers, piercing, warm sunlight, and deep, cold clouds, the light and color temperature shifted throughout our 30-minute conversation and photo shoot. Spending extra time with all of Tyler’s show bikes unfurls the builder’s intent with his brand. Making custom, one-off bikes is time-intensive, and being a one-person shop doesn’t afford him the ability to open a build queue these days. So he spends extra time with these show bikes, used to showcase his creative thinking and practical execution of a bricolage of machined and 3D sintered components.

Tyler, it was good to see you out of your comfort zone, outside of your hometown, and experimenting with creative solutions for common problems. Who knows if the bars will be available and when, but the fact that they exist is extra special. Enjoy Japan homie!

@BTCHNBikes

Cherubim NJS Keirin Racer

Japanese craftsmanship, design, and tradition, all rolled into one bike. Cherubim’s Shinichi Konno built this bike in 2016 for Yuichiro Kamiyama, the highest earning Keirin racer in Japanese history. Keirin, for the uninitiated, is a form of motor-paced track bicycle racing originating in Japan in 1948.

Keirin racing follows Japan’s JKA racing format, in which tactical team formations cooperate before breaking away for the final sprint. Components used in Keirin require NJS certification and can be denoted by a special NJS stamp in place. Builders also must follow this certification, and it is an honor to achieve the label. Keirin is also a legal, government-regulated public gambling sport. Racers can earn a healthy living, with riders like Yuichiro Kamiyama raking in over 229,907,532 yen over his career.

As Yuichiro Kamiyama’s racing pedigree has earned him a lot of yen, Konno-san mixed gold flake glitter into the clear coat of the frame. Paired with Cherubim’s meticulously crafted lugwork and NJS-certified construction, this bike embodies Japanese construction and heritage.

I was lucky enough to have Konno-san magically appear outside while shooting his bike for a portrait.

@Cherubim

Curve Big Kev 32er Prototype 1

This was the first Big Kev that Melbourne, Australia-based Curve Cycling built to test out the emerging 32er wheelset. First debuted at the Spoken event in Australia, the bike has since undergone a stunning turquoise paint job, laid down by Candy Factory Paintworks, operated by co-founder Steve Varga. The second prototype was displayed at the 2026 Bespoked Dresden show.

Built around a 2.4″ tire with clearance for more, the Big Kev 32er features a Mone trip-plane fork and is built from a mixture of Columbus tubing. A special chainstay yoke ensures tire, chainring, and q-factor alignment without the need for obtuse crimping and the chopped seat stay ends terminate at the top tube in a bed of brass.

Once again, Curve displays its abilities, and Jimmy brings the heat!

@CurveCycling

Yanagi Kazusa Adventure Gravel Bike

Kamagaya City, Japan-based Yanagi brought one of its Kazusa adventure gravel bikes to the 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase. This bike is the result of extensive collaboration between builder Koichi Iizumi and Sukiyaki Bikes, who did the custom pantography on the White Industries cranks. Then, as the final touch, Rintaro Shimoyama from Ghooost did the hand lettering over the plating, which was done by Nitto.

The talent of Sukiyaki is on full display here, with elaborate panto carvings in the White cranks, which took the artist two months to complete. The other parts on the bike – the stem spacer, headset cap, and head badge took another few months to complete.

Upon completion, this bike embodies what is so wonderful about the small maker community, particularly in Japan. Three talented makers coming together, working on a bike – which was plated by the legends at Nitto – all for a special show like Bespoked Osaka.

There was a great reverence felt with these talented humans. Myself for their craft and them for my hard work documenting it. Moments like this bring an intense sense of honor and pride for what we do over here at The Radavist: two decades of love and reverence for the global maker community.

Sugoi! Yanagi, Sukiyaki, Rintaro.

@Yanagi @Sukiyaki @Ghooost

The Radavist thanks Circles Japan for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Osaka coverage and our independent Reportage!

The post 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 02: Alps, BTCHN, Cherubim, Curve, Yanagi appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Fitbit Edge In-Depth Review: Worth the Upgrade?
entry.content:
<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Fitbit Edge could most easily be called the Fitbit Charge 7, but sometimes switching things up is a good refresh for companies and brands, and so here we are. In many ways, the Fitbit Edge will feel very familiar to Fitbit Charge users, yet it’ll concurrently feel very much like a recent Google Pixel Watch. That’s both good and bad. There are a lot of good things coming from the Pixel Watch 5 & Fitbit Air that have landed here. Yet equally, having used it the past few weeks, there are a number of smaller things that aren’t quite what we had on the very popular Fitbit Charge series.

Speaking of which, both my wife and I have been using Fitbit Edge units over this last while on all of our workouts. Runs, rides, hikes, walks, gym stuff, and everything in between. With that, let’s dive into what’s new, and then all my daily and workout usage experiences.

What’s New:

The Fitbit Edge is the next version of the Fitbit Charge 6, which came out in 2023. Here’s how it’s different:

– Increased screen/display by 46% (has 1.34” display)
– Case thickness is 11.5mm
– Added physical side button that actually clicks (previous was just a touch area)
– Added altimeter (for stair tracking, as well as elevation tracking)
– Added automatic workout detection (now supports 100 sports)
– Increased supported manual workout profiles to 50 workout profiles
– Made user-replaceable/serviceable battery (the first Fitbit-branded product to do so)
– GPS accuracy improvement claimed at 40% more accurate (via new GPS chipset, and new aluminum case design)
– Switched to a more modern user interface, matching the Pixel Watch 5 series
– Added structured workout support
– Added support for dual usage with Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air (e.g., switching back and forth seamlessly)
– Added fast charging (5 minutes gets you 1 day of usage)
– Removed Google Pay (NFC Contactless payments)
– Removed EDA Scan feature (but does have continuous stress monitoring in the background)
– Changed the band attachment mechanism (old Fitbit habits die hard)
– Switched the charger to the same charger as the Fitbit Air (hey, at least they picked something else they already had this time)
– Added a bunch of band accessory types
– Price increased to $179 (officially the Charge 6 was $159 previously, but realistically it sat between $99 and $129 virtually all the time)
– Also a Stephen Curry model at $219 (US, Canada, EMEA)

In terms of some other general specs, just for recap purposes:

– Same claimed 7-day battery life
– Still has heart rate broadcasting feature via Bluetooth (though it can be a bit funky in terms of compatibility)
– Still has music control of your phone’s music (no onboard music storage)
– Still has Google Maps turn-by-turn directions (with phone)
– Still has smartphone notifications (more integration on Android than iOS)
– Still has full sleep tracking
– Still has continuous heart rate monitoring (background and workout)
– Still supports high & low heart rate alerts
– Supports the Google Health Guardian features announced a few months ago
– You can do quick replies on Android, though not on iOS devices
– Has FDA/EU approved medical ECG functionality, including background Afib detection
– Includes skin temperature sensor
– Supports Steps, Distance, Active Zone Minutes, VO2Max, Floor/elevation, Cardio Load, and many more metrics
– Two sizes of bands (see specs below)
– Water resistance level is 5ATM, and IP68 for dust protection

So that covers the piles of new stuff, and some of the bits that were there before. But there are still numerous color schemes/models to choose from.

Model Options & Detailed Specs:

The Fitbit Air case comes in 5 different colorways, and then with that, a huge slate of band options. Starting off with the core options you can buy, they are as follows:

– Matte Black Aluminum case / Obsidian Active Band
– Polished Silver Aluminum case / Fog Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Olive Active Band
– Champagne Gold case / Canyon Active Band
– Satin Pyrite Aluminum case / Stephen Curry Special Edition

From there, you’ve got the following band types/options:

– Active Band
– Active Sport band
– Metal Link band
– Magnet band
– Performance Loop

Now, for most of our testing (my wife and I), we’ve been wearing the relatively basic/default Active band, which works perfectly fine and is easy to adjust/etc.

Still, we both wore other bands as well. Yesterday we had a fancy afternoon thing to go to, and swapped out to the Metal Link band. Hers was the champagne gold, and mine the brushed silver. Obviously neither quite perfectly matched with the models we had, but…well…that’s the models we had:

My only complaint here is that I found the clasp release button could actually get reasonably easily pressed. Ironically, it didn’t happen all day during most of the day, and then towards the end of the day, it was triggering constantly. My wife didn’t have this issue, so….yeah.

I’ve also worn the Active Sport band a bit, though I didn’t honestly find it all that meaningfully different than the Active band, in terms of sport wearability.

And finally, I have the Magnet Band, which is super cool and just snaps tight/shut.

Finally, looking at the tech specs, here’s a whole slate of things that may or may not be interesting to you:

– Display is 1.34”/34mm AMOLED display, supporting an always-on configuration
– Display supports adjustable brightness
– Bluetooth 5.4
– Processor: Ambiq AP5 MCU
– GPS chipset supports GPS+Galileo in US, and GPS+Galileo+GLONASS+BeiDou+QZSS outside of US
– Onboard memory: 64MB NOR flash memory, 7 days of detailed motion data (minute intervals), 30 days of daily totals, heart rate at 2-second intervals
– Internal sensors: Altimeter, Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Red and infrared sensors for oxygen saturation (SpO2), Multipurpose electrical sensors compatible with ECG app, Photoplethysmography (PPG) optical heart rate sensor, Ambient light sensor, Far-field skin temperature sensor
– Battery is 65mAh
– Fully end-user replaceable battery
– Charging speed: 5 minutes of fast charging for 1 day of battery life, or 100% in 90 minutes
– Requires iOS 16.4 or newer, and Android 11 or newer
– Fitbit Edge Weight: 17.7g without band
– Fitbit Edge Dimensions: 39.22 x 25.56 mm
– Fitbit Edge Height/Thickness: 11.58mm
– Case is made from 100% recycled aluminum
– Active band: Silicone with “soft-touch coating”
– Active Band Sizing: Small fits wrists 130-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band: “Recycled polyester yarns with water-repellent coating and stainless steel lugs, as well as a raised interior print for increased airflow.”
– Stephen Curry band sizing (US): Small fits wrists 135-170mm around, Large fits 170-210mm around
– Stephen Curry band sizing (EU/Canada): Single-size fits wrists 150-195mm around
– Water resistance: 5ATM/50 meters
– Dust immersion resistance: IP68

Phew, got all that? Good, let’s roll right into the basics of the unit day to day.

The Daily Usage Basics:

In this section, I’ll go through all the daily usage basics of the Fitbit Edge, like activity/step tracking, sleep tracking, and general health bits. Then after this I’ll cover workout pieces.

First up is interacting with the device. The Fitbit Edge gained a physical button on the right side, which quickly opens the apps menu, for things like accessing the alarms, ECG, exercise, media controls, and weather. Previously on the Fitbit Charge 6, this was a touch-sensitive area, but not a clicking button:

The button is great, and I’ve been super happy with it. Note that at present, long-pressing it doesn’t do anything.

Instead, for most other interactions, you’ll use the touchscreen, which allows you to swipe left/right/up/down, and tap it for what you need. Of course, the first thing you’ll see is your watch face:

You can customize these in the Google Health App, allowing you to save multiple watch faces to the Fitbit Edge for quick swapping between them. You can customize each of the complications (data bits) on the watch face, as well as the coloring. There’s roughly a dozen watch faces to choose from:

You can swipe down anytime to access the controls menu. This includes things like the flashlight, do-not-disturb mode, heart rate broadcasting, and more. I’ll cover some of these in more depth throughout the review.

Instead, if we swipe from the right, we’ll get the quick start menu for workouts, allowing us to access the most recent sport profiles:

Swipe again, and we’ve got a high-level overview of the Focus Metrics panel:

This one (above) is kinda odd, though, in that you have to tap into it again to get to a longer list of focus metrics:

However, the oddest part here is that you can’t tap any of these metrics to see more details on-device. For example, want to see what time it thinks you went to sleep or woke up? Can’t do that here. Have to go to the phone. Want to see why your Readiness Score is what it is? Can’t do that here. Have to go to the phone.

In discussions with Google/Fitbit, they seem to hint that changes are coming here in this area. I sure hope so, as this seems pretty half-finished at best.

In any case, as you keep swiping through these to the left/right, you’ll essentially see other data metrics for stuff I already showed in the Focus Metrics. For example, swipe again, and you’ll see the very small sleep tidbits. You can’t tap into this, though, for any additional details beyond what you see below:

Same goes for heart metrics:

And then there’s weather, showing current weather in your area, and then another page for quick access to the timers:

And finally, there’s another page for media controls. There is no music storage on the Fitbit Edge, which seems logical/fine to me. However, what’s less logical is the lack of NFC/payment support. This was in the Fitbit Charge 6 and has been in countless cheaper Fitbit devices over the years, yet it’s not here. Given Google doesn’t support the higher-end Pixel Watch series on iOS, this means there’s really no option for iOS users to use a Google device if they want contactless payments. And as both Google and Apple know well, very few people are going to change phone platforms merely to support a wearable. That ship sailed long, long ago.

Google did provide a bit of color as to why they cut the contactless payment support, saying:

“Fitbit Edge does not offer NFC for payments. It was not widely used by our Charge 6 users – in fact, less than 1% used the feature on Charge 6 – so we prioritized other top features such as adding a sleek design, altimeter and week long battery.” – Andy Abramson (Head of Product at Google Health)

And to be fair, I wouldn’t necessarily disagree with that line of thinking, though ultimately, I still think the lack of iOS option for higher-end Google wearables is really the core issue here.

In any case, since we can’t see many details on the screen itself beyond core metrics, a lot of that is shifted to your phone and the Google Health app (the Fitbit app is dead; long live the Fitbit app!). Here you can see your summary at the top for the day, in terms of steps, readiness scores, sleep, and cardio load for the week. This is all free. However, anytime you see lots of descriptive text, that’ll be part of Google’s Premium subscription. In other words, the data is free, but the wordy analysis requires a subscription.

Looking at my sleep metrics, for example from last night, those look accurate and have been consistently accurate over the last few weeks. The only one that caused many wearables to stumble was yesterday’s daylight saving time change, which seemed to truncate an hour of sleep. However, otherwise the times I woke up and went to sleep have been spot-on.

Note that I don’t compare accuracy of sleep stages/phases, as that’s simply not an accurate metric. In a best-case setting for so-called gold-standard devices, those basically top out in the mid-80% accuracy range, which is pretty poor for a gold-standard device to compare against. Thus, I’m not going to mislead you here.

Instead, I will get annoyed at one sleep-related thing that Google/Fitbit lacks on the Fitbit Edge, which is automatic sleep mode toggles. Specifically, while you can set up sleep schedules and do-not-disturb schedules, that actually won’t prevent the screen from illuminating all crazy-pants in the middle of the night (or, perhaps lack of pants in the middle of the night). Instead, anytime the sheets or you brush the screen, it’ll light up. Same goes for raise-to-wake. Which is both annoying and a long-solved problem on wearables.

Instead, you need to tap the bed icon each night to force it into sleep mode. That by itself isn’t actually as annoying to me as remembering again in the morning to un-tap that bed icon, so that things like raise-to-wake actually work. Again, like the other details piece, I get the impression there’s a fast-follow to enable this on the Fitbit Edge, but it does feel like the Google/Fitbit team is just a bit behind on getting this device fully baked.

In any case, beyond that, within the Google Health app you’ve also got the Health Status panel, which shows your trending metrics over the course of longer time periods:

There does appear to be a bug here in that my Blood Oxygen levels have been updating nightly, both on the Fitbit Edge since putting it on, as well as for months on other devices, but since wearing the Fitbit Edge, it’s stopped trending for me. This is a minor nit for me, though it does make my metrics ‘4 out of 5’, instead of ‘5 out of 5’.

When it comes to text notifications, note that you’ll see those come in on the device, though on iOS you’ll be unable to respond to them. But you can read them and clear them:

Finally, in terms of charging, you’ve got the same charger as the Fitbit Air, so kudos to the Google/Fitbit team for managing to keep the same charger for more than one product. I can only assume they had a grand celebration for finally unlocking that accomplishment, complete with Haribo gummy bears and rosé wine. Well deserved.

Indeed, you can fast-charge silly-quick to get you through the day/night. And in terms of battery life, if you leave it with the default gesture-based display, it seems to be on trend for the week-long battery life. However, I quickly changed it to always-on display, and that pulls things back real-quick to basically two days of battery life. Again, all dependent on how much GPS-outside workout time you have. With that, let’s talk sweaty stuff.

Sports & Workouts:

The Fitbit Edge takes virtually all of the best features from the recently launched screenless Fitbit Air (which is basically a Whoop competitor), and rolls them into the Fitbit Edge. This means that you’ve got equal parts manual activity/workout controls, as well as the ability to just totally ignore the unit on your wrist, and know that it’ll track things behind the scenes automatically. Both my wife and I have done both. Sometimes manually starting a workout, and other times just letting it figure it out.

Starting off with the manual side, to begin a workout you’ll tap either from the watch face (if the complication is enabled), or just swipe once from the right to the sport menu:

Here you can choose from your most recently used sports, or one of the ones in the list. On the manual workout profile side, here are the workout profiles that are supported on the Fitbit Edge. Note these are a subset of the automatic detection list, which is around 100 activities (see following this):

Manually Selectable Sport Profiles

Aerobics
Badminton
Baseball
Basketball
Bike
Bootcamp
Boxing
Canoeing
Circuit training
Core training
Cricket
Cross-country ski
CrossFit
Dancing
Elliptical
Field hockey
Football
Golf
HIIT
Hike
Indoor climbing
Kayaking
Kickboxing
Martial arts
Mountain bike
Open swim
Outdoor workout
Paddleboarding
Padel
Pickleball
Pilates
Pool swim
Powerlifting
Rollerblading
Rowing machine
Rugby
Run
Skating
Skiing
Snowboarding
Soccer
Spinning
Sport
Stair climber
Strength training
Surfing
Swim
Tennis
Treadmill run
Walk
Weightlifting
Weights
Workout
Yoga

I definitely appreciate having all of these profiles available on-device, rather than just a very basic set. Which I suppose is the general trend in watches/wearables the last year or two: More workout profile options is better.

Once you’ve selected a sport profile, there are a few options you can choose, such as any targets or goals like distance, pace (high/low), calories, etc.

Additionally, there’s the option for GPS usage. This allows you to leverage GPS internal to the Fitbit Edge, or to use it from your phone. The choice is honestly pretty simple: Which device’s battery do you want to burn? By default, even when you toggle GPS on for an activity (like a run), it’ll default to using your phone’s GPS (via Bluetooth).

However, within the settings of the Google Health app, you can choose to instead use the device’s GPS. By default, it’ll be on ‘Dynamic’, which Google has confirmed actually translates to “use the phone unless the phone isn’t there”.

In my case, as seen above, I switched to ‘Built-in’. This is the configuration I mostly used it within. In my testing, I’d burn the Fitbit Edge battery at about 15%/hour, for outdoor GPS workouts with the screen in always-on display.

However, if you want to save some battery, in gesture-based mode, I got a fair bit longer. Basically twice as much for this 5-hour ride in the mountains, burning at roughly 8%/hour:

In the above example, the battery started at 90%, though it ended at 50%.

Speaking of which, the Google Health app does support mirroring of data from the Fitbit Edge to your phone, if you want to use it as a bike computer or just generally see your workout data metrics on your phone in real time. This isn’t super detailed, nor does it show as much data as on the device itself, but it’s an option for the core bits.

Still, circling all the way back to the start of the workout, you’ll see your GPS status icon at the top:

Once you start, you’ll see your data details across a few different data pages:

That said, quirkily, you can’t change/modify any of the data pages from a sports standpoint. They are what they are.

Nonetheless, all of this works reasonably well within a workout, and I had no issues there in terms of general usage. For things like rain during workouts, this made the screen pretty tough to use for swipes specifically; that was also true of other wearables I was testing at the time.

Once you’ve completed your workout, you’ll see summary data of the workout:

And then over on the Google Health app, you can see more details of it:

One of the metrics you’ve probably noticed a few times is the ‘Cardio Load’. This is essentially your training load, and it resets every week. You accumulate Cardio Load during workouts, and roughly speaking, you get more Cardio Load the higher your heart rate is. So, on an easy walk with no meaningfully raised heart rate, you might accumulate just 0 or 1 cardio load. Yet a flat-out balls-to-the-wall 5KM run might score a few hundred units of cardio load. You can see this on the Fitbit Edge itself after a workout, as well as in summary stats.

Your goal dynamically changes each week, based on your personal historical data, as well as any goals that you might have configured in the Google Coach features (those are Premium features).

Otherwise, you can simply see how it compares to your historical data within the Google Health app:

Next, as mentioned, you can push a structured workout to the Fitbit Edge. This is a notable upgrade from the Fitbit Charge 6, which didn’t support structured workouts. However, it’s a little bit different than on a Pixel Watch, where you select it on the watch. Here, you’ll need to select it from within the Google Health app. This can be workouts that Google has created for you, or ones you create yourself:

Then, you’ll choose to start it from the phone, rather than on the Fitbit Edge. All of the instructions will be on your phone, not on the Fitbit Edge. The Edge is basically just recording and showing your general data. The phone is where everything is explained. This is perfectly logical for indoor/gym/yoga/etc. workouts, but it’s kinda wonky for an interval workout outside, where you need to keep checking your phone for what you should be doing. I’m not a huge fan of this implementation, especially if you’re a runner.

Finally, and semi-unrelated, if you are indoors and want to broadcast your heart rate to other devices, you can do so with the heart rate broadcast option by swiping down from the top and activating the heart rate broadcast icon. An example here would be pairing it to a Peloton Bike to use as a heart rate sensor/strap:

Note that Fitbit’s implementation doesn’t actually follow the Secure Bluetooth pairing standard, so it won’t really work with everything else out there unless they specifically partnered with Fitbit. For example, it works with Peloton and Zwift, but not with a Garmin Edge bike computer (sadly, the two Edges can’t chat). Sigh.

Of course, everything I’ve talked about thus far is about manually starting workouts and basically interacting with your Fitbit Edge. But the other way to do workouts is just to do them, and not even touch the Fitbit Edge (of course, still wear it). That then leverages Automatic Workout Detection, which is pulled from the Fitbit Air launched earlier this year.

Within that realm, there are basically two different ways the Fitbit Edge will detect workouts. The first set of workout types are ones it “really knows” and should get right each time. Whereas the second set are ones it takes a flyer on, based on historical data, and hopes for the best with an educated guess. Here’s the first set:

Core Automatically Detected sports without any context:

Outdoor Walk
Outdoor Run
Outdoor Bike
Stationary Bike
Elliptical
Rowing Machine
Swim
Racket Sports
Rowing
Golf
Basketball
Soccer
Strength Training
Sports (generic – team sports)
‘Activity’ (generic – periods of sustained elevated HR)

Then this next set requires some sort of historical context, as well as previous confirmations of the activity in the app. In other words, if it knows that you mow the lawn every Saturday morning, and then do hoeing on Saturday evening, it’ll likely detect those automatically each weekend if it feels the movement patterns are similar enough to your past hoeing activities:

Context-required Automatic Detection Types:

I do want to point out that I’d love to have been a fly on the wall in conference rooms at Google when they debated putting the ‘Hoeing’ activity type in there.

While I cannot attest to the Hoeing activity accuracy levels, I can say that when it comes to other things it detected, it had no problems for me or my wife, in terms of detecting walks, hikes, and indoor cycling rides. When you do these activities, it’ll show up very similar, but slightly different than a regular activity. First, there won’t be any GPS tracks associated with it (even if outdoors). It doesn’t automatically turn that on. But second, you can actually change the times if it truncates something incorrectly.

While Fitbit had some basic automatic detection in the Charge 6, it’s nowhere near what they’re doing now with the Fitbit Edge. So this is definitely a bit of a step up.

With that, let’s take a look at the workout accuracy of both heart rate and GPS.

Accuracy:

The prior-gen Fitbit Charge 6 was known as a hot mess of a dumpster fire when it came to heart rate and GPS accuracy. As a user, you basically had two options: You could loosen up the band and get decent GPS accuracy, but nonsense heart rate accuracy. Or, you could tighten the band and get no usable GPS track at all, but good heart rate accuracy. Choosing both was simply not an option, due to a design that put the GPS antenna on the underside edges of the Charge 6.

One of the big things called out by Google with the Fitbit Edge is addressing that issue. The question is, does it?

Let’s start off with an indoor trainer ride. This one isn’t too hard, with some moderate but not crazy intervals. Here we can see that it really struggled at the beginning, for no obvious reason. It wasn’t until the main set started that it locked on.

I’m a bit surprised by this, as this should have been easy-town. That said, once it started the workout, it was largely fine.

Next, looking at heart rate on a bit under a 45-minute outdoor ride (mostly pavement,  tiny bit of gravel towards the end), we can see it struggles a bit at the beginning. To be fair, this was downhill on this first section, which many wearables will struggle starting with. By around the 10-minute marker, I’ve stabilized on flat ground, and you can see it largely trends OK, until round the 35-minute marker, where it struggles a little bit.

If we look at the GPS tracks on this, at a high level it looks very similar to the Garmin Edge 1060 and COROS Dura 2 I had on my handlebars then:

If we zoom in to a fast descent section, the Fitbit Edge (using built-in GPS), actually manages to stick on this road better than the $550 COROS Dura 2.

Though, on this much slower 20% grade climb, the Fitbit Edge wobbled a bit more than the others. It’s interesting that the section it wobbled (just below the pools), is actually the portion I had to get off the bike for a few seconds, as the recent rainstorms had basically washed away a portion of this gravel road, making brief impassable sections when trying to go up.

Lastly, if we look at the elevation profile on this, using the barometric altimeter inside the unit, it was quite close here, within just a couple of meters most of the time:

Looking at another ride, this one a 90-minute ride that was a mix of road and gravel, you can see things are…umm… a bit mixed when it comes to heart rate. Though, the Suunto Run 2 also struggled here on heart rate. Yes, you can see things ‘roughly trended’ in the right way, but overall this is a bit prickly.

On the GPS side of things, overall it was pretty good, occasionally slightly offset a meter or two from the other units when I’d do some lower-speed swerves, but still a *massive* improvement over the Fitbit Charge 6, which wouldn’t track GPS to save its life.

But you can see places like these straightaways here; it’s spot-on with the other GPS units, including $800 bike computers:

Finally, looking at a run from today, this is a simple 5KM run through both trails and pavement, split roughly evenly. Here’s the heart rate side first. This looks reasonably good. A few minor quibbles, but overall pretty solid despite being up/down on steep terrain; things are good here.

And then looking at the GPS, here’s the wide look at things:

Looking closely at some parts in the trees, and a bit of a ravine, it’s not meaningfully different than the $1,199 Garmin Fenix 9 Pro inReach model, or the $399 Suunto Run 2.

Same goes for this section here. Virtually indistinguishable.

Overall, this is a massive upgrade over the Fitbit Charge 6 for both heart rate and GPS. With the Charge 6, you had to ‘choose one’ of the two to be accurate. Here, the GPS is more than good enough for most things, and the heart rate is OK (though not great). The unit lacks the size/space to put in Google’s much better optical HR sensor found in the Pixel Watch 5, so instead it leans on a smaller sensor that fits into this case. Still, I suspect for most people interested in this device for probably more casual workout tracking, this is probably good enough.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Final Thoughts:

For the vast majority of users, the Fitbit Edge will be a notable upgrade over the Fitbit Charge 6. Or definitely a Fitbit Charge 5. The GPS & heart rate situation is vastly improved, the user interface is cleaner and easier to understand, and I think the majority of the Google Health app is an improvement (though obviously, there are still some folks that prefer the older Fitbit app, especially if you don’t plan on being a Premium subscriber).

That said, while none of the issues I ran into were major blockers, it definitely lacks a bit of software finishing polish around the edges. Specifically, things like not having the automatic sleep mode for the display, not being able to tap into any of the metrics on the unit itself for more details, and then not being able to customize workout data pages. The way Google implemented these seems like they had grander/deeper plans, but eventually cut their losses for a holiday season launch. It sounds like some things are planned for firmware updates down the road.

Still, for a sub-$180 device targeted more at wellness than hardcore athletes, it largely fits the bill for tracking and analyzing your daily workouts, your daily health/sleep, and doing so in a tidy form factor that’s easy to understand. Having the automatic workout detection is super handy for when you don’t want to fuss with the screen, and yet it’ll properly track everything behind the scenes.

With that, thanks for reading!

entry.title: 2026 Bespoked Osaka Picks 01: Après, D3, Project D, Prova, Sour, Tailfin, Vigore – John Watson
entry.content:
Maido from Osaka! Cari and John were in attendance at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka event, where they documented a variety of bikes from the global framebuilding community. Read on for a look at the Bespoked Osaka venue and a selection of builders including Après, D3, Project D, Prova, Sour/Tailfin, and Vigore…

Bespoked Osaka

For the first time, Bespoked, the largest handmade bike show in the world, landed in Japan, setting its eyes on the city of Osaka. This port city has a low-key vibe compared to Tokyo, with a vibrant cycling scene and reverence for craft, style, and functionality. For its venue, Bespoked chose the Glion Museum, which is home to classic and modern cars from around the globe.

This 10,000-square-meter property consists of four buildings, two of which were used to house the Bespoked showcase. It was built in 1923 originally as a port authority and features pre-war brick and timber construction. Bespoked settled into  two adjacent buildings the Thursday before the showcase and come Friday morning, it was bustling with builders and industry attendees.

On display was a mixture of classic road and touring bikes, built to the highest Japanese standards, to experimental designs from Europe, and just about everything in between. My intent with this showcase coverage was to pay homage to the builders of Japan, while still highlighting some of the global attendees. I hope you enjoy my Picks 01.

Velo Après Touring Bike

Velo Après makes classic-lined French-inspired touring and randonneuring bicycles. With two trim options available, the “Standard” comes nicely equipped with Shimano Claris for around $3,000 US, or the “Special” with a higher-end groupset and saddle for around $3,500. Those prices are for complete bikes.

Raijin Works makes these frames by hand, to the Velo Après specifications with ten colors to choose from, disc or rim configuration, and seven set sizes. Special add-ons are available, such as this stunning front randonneuring rack, rear racks, or other touring accouterments.

Japanese Kasai tubing is used to ensure the proper ride feel with a fork that planes and a frame that dances with you on your ride. Bang for buck, this bike is hard to beat.

@VeloAprès

D3 Lab Moridge Hardtail Cargo Bike

Beijing-based D3 Lab was the first bike at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka showcase that caught my eye. Ok, that’s an understatement. It blew me away. The two minds behind D3 Lab, Du and Joe, were putting the finishing touches on the bike as I was admiring the end-of-day golden-hour light at the Glion Museum. Still working out my photo setup, I wheeled the bike out into the expanse of the pre-war brick facility, looking for a quiet corner to poke and prod this creation with my lens.

This bricolage assemblage utilizes two distinct construction techniques, meshing traditional tubing brazing with laser-cut truss framing for the front platform’s structure. Inspired by triple triangle track bikes, the seat tube is kinked, and the seat stays dropped, allowing the wheel to be tucked in close towards the bottom bracket, making it incredibly nimble and maneuverable. The 120 mm travel shock keeps the front end impact resistant when carrying a load.

For steering, rather than using a push rod, the Moridge utilizes a cable steering mechanism, which allows for adjustment vis-à-vis barrel adjusters.

Its name, “Moridge,” is a combination of “Mobile Bridge,” as the front truss support is inspired by Arete Structures commonly used in bridge design. The frame is powder-coated, with the brown parts all Cerakote. The colors were selected by the bag maker, Cyclofowl. The bag maker also designed a comic for D3 Lab showcasing the brand’s origin story: a crashed alien ship, which is also depicted on the head tube badge.

Various components like the Redshift ShockStop post were stripped and Cerakoted, designed to pair with the D3 Labs stem and riser bar. Truss spandrel triangles are incorporated throughout the frame and bags.

Du and Joe, it was a pleasure to meet you. I’m so elated with how these photos came out, and it was a really special evening spent documenting your work.

@D3Lab

Project D Lustra Low Pro Track Bike

In Latin, Lustra translates to a summary of your skill set, and in Polish, it means mirrored. For Łódź, Poland-based Project D, a brainchild of engineer Dominik Dominiak, the word couldn’t be a better-suited label for his stunning low pro track bike. Full stop. This is the most stunning bicycle I have documented this year, and these photos are echelon-level for someone who has spent his life turning a camera to the work of framebuilders.

Dominik was inspired to begin building bikes by a red Cherubim bike, built by the master Shinichi Konno, he saw at a NAHBS event one year. So when Bespoked announced its Osaka showcase, he got to sketching a design. His intent was to create one continuous line from the fork to the top tube, which would then shift to the seat stays, chainstays, and bifurcate into the seat and downtube.

While the saddle-to-bar drop looks aggressive, it’s actually based on Dominik’s road bike fit, placing his hands in the same position as the drops on his bike. Utilizing bullhorns allows him to lower the top tube considerably, giving the appearance of an aggressive fit, even though it is very comfortable. Unfortunately, he didn’t have pedals with him to ride the bike…

The bike’s mastery lies in the execution of the bullhorn bars and the steering assembly, which rotates around a radius without interrupting the visual lines of the frame. All of the seams are concealed on the back of the head tube, leaving the front of the bike void of any bolts or interruptions.

It took seven layers of paint to give the Lustra its red glow. The seat tube’s teardrop profile creates a stark visual line at the rear, while side reflections minimize its visual heft, giving it the appearance of a sword’s edge, intended to slice through the air.

Yes, this is innovation and art, but it is a functional bicycle with operable parts and beautiful, jaw-dropping design notes everywhere. The track and fork ends are the most elegant I’ve seen, and the entire bicycle is what one ought to expect from shows like Bespoked. Meeting Dominik was a real pleasure. Documenting his work was a dream.

If you fancy the Lustra, it is for sale. Contact Dominik for inquiries. As a more personal note, it was a real joy to connect with Dominik and document his work to the best of my ability. You’re one talented human, friend.

@ProjectDBicycles

Prova Evoluto Road

Melbourne-based Prova Cycles is the collective effort between Mark and Kelly Hester, two siblings obsessed with creating the world’s finest titanium bicycles. Together with Dan Knives of Superbe Velo Service, a master wheel builder who also builds each Prova for its customers, and the talented painters at Velo Craft, Prova continuously evolves its modus operandi. Debuting at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show is the latest evolutionary step in its road design, the Evoluto.

The Evoluto is Prova’s take on the ultimate modern metal bike. It takes the learning of the Integrale and Speciale road platforms and adds a unique headtube and bottom bracket design. Mark designs each model in CAD, paying attention to using spline lines to create a visual edge that ties the bike’s form from the head tube all the way to the dropouts.

Since a Prova is custom, the Evoluto can be designed to clear either 35 mm or 40 mm tires, and the bike can be fitted with either an Enve integrated carbon fork or the Prova titanium fork. Extra effort was put in place on this bike’s wheels, with Dan Knives polishing the DT 180 hubs, to which Mark then etched the logos back onto the surface.

Known for its simple paint designs and ombré fades, Prova’s first foray into graphics is present with this Evoluto, which displays circular box lining, inspired by Japanese fans. Velo Craft’s expertise is on full display here, with impeccable linework and masking. The clearcoat’s 2 mm edging ensures the classic Japanese-inspired design stays tack sharp for years to come.

Mark, it’s always a pleasure to document you and your team’s work. Kelly, we wish you were here. Mark looks lonely in this hardstyle pose without you!

@ProvaCycles

Sour x Tailfin

For the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show, Tailfin’s marketing director James Bracey worked with Dresden, Germany-based Sour Bicycles to create a one-of-a-kind finish for its Space Cake all-road bike. Inspired by cumulonimbus clouds, illuminated by an ombré fade at sunset, this paint job transitions from lavender to pink, from top to bottom.

The bike is accessorized with custom R&D Tailfin bags, which display the aluminum structures of each model. Bracey added that customers have requested these bags before, for ease of locating their packed items.

Tailfin’s R&D bags are always a showstopper, and when teaming up with Sour Bicycles, it’s a winning combination.

@SourBicycles @Tailfin

Vigore Kyoto Yuki’s Road Bike

Kyoto-based Vigore was founded in 1929 as a bicycle shop called Kataoka Bicycle Shokai. In 1968, Shiro Kataoka began building bikes under the Vigore banner at that shop. Now, Masato Kataoka and his daughter Yuki are the only bespoke framebuilders in Kyoto. On display at the 2026 Bespoked Osaka show was Yuki’s new road bike, a bike she built from start to finish.

Yuki learned to build five years ago from her father, and she’s been thinking of the perfect road bike ever since she first learned the art of lugged framebuilding. She designed this bike to fit shorter riders, maintaining clean proportions of larger-sized bikes, while relying on 650b wheels. The profile and silhouette is incredibly balanced, and the bike’s smooth pedaling demeanor is ensured thanks to the slightly higher bottom bracket.

Kyoto is surrounded by mountains, so Yuki wanted a bike that could use modern groupsets. It’s designed with UDH dropouts, so customers can select a full-mount Sram kit, or a 2x setup from Shimano. The bike uses disc brakes for comfortable braking down mountain passes and the elegant bend to the fork is a nod to traditional road bikes.

Yuki and her father embody the Japanese tradition of passing down knowledge from one generation to the next. Vigore’s passion and precision framebuilding were on full display at the 2026 Bespoked Showcase…

@VigoreKyoto

 

The Radavist thanks Circles Japan for sponsoring our 2026 Bespoked Osaka coverage and our independent Reportage!
